case_name: Ontario English Catholic Teachers' Assn v. Ontario (Attorney General)
text:
Ontario

Supreme Court

Ontario
English Catholic Teachers’ Assn v.
Ontario
(Attorney General)

Date: 1998-07-22

Ontario
English Catholic Teachers’ Association et
al.

and

Attorney General of

Ontario
;
Ontario
Catholic
School
Trustees’ Association et al., Interveners

Ontario
Public School Boards’ Association et al.

and

Attorney General of
Ontario; Association des conseillers (ères) des écoles publiques de l’Ontario
et al., Interveners

Court File Nos.
97-CV-137668; 98-CV-139317

Ontario
Court (General Division) Cumming J.

Heard: June 17,
18, 19, 22, 23, 24 and 26, 1998

Judgment
rendered:
July 22, 1998

Paul Cavalluzzo, Fay C. Faraday and Karen
Schucher, for applicants, Ontario English Catholic Teachers’ Association,
Marshall Jarvis, Claire Ross and Annemarie Ross.

Brian A. Kelsey, Q.C., and John P Bell,
for applicants, Ontario Public School Boards’ Association, and the Toronto District School Board.

Michael A. Hines, for applicants, Ontario
Public School Boards’ Association, Upper Grand District School Board, Elizabeth
Sandals, and Joleene Kemp.

Maurice A. Green, for applicants, Ontario
Secondary School Teachers’ Federation, David Edwards and Robert Churchill.

Elizabeth J. Shilton, for applicants,
Federation of Women Teachers’ Associations of Ontario and Ontario Public
School Teachers’ Federation.

Janet E. Minor, Michel Y. Hélie and
Robert E. Charney, for respondent.

Peter D. Lauwers and John C. Murray, for
intervener, Ontario Catholic School Trustees’ Association.

Paul S. Rouleau, John C. Murray and M.
Sean Gaudet for interveners, Association Franco‑Ontarienne des conseils
scolaires Catholiques and Association des conseillers (ères) des écoles
publiques de l’Ontario.

Michael A. Hines, for intervener, Annie
Kidder.

CUMMING J.:—

Overview

[
1
]

The applicants in the two applications before the Court seek
declarations that various parts of the
Education Quality Improvement Act,
1997,
S.O. 1997, c. 31 (“
Bill 160
”), are unconstitutional, and of no
force and effect.
Bill 160
was enacted December 1, 1997, resulting in various
amendments to the
Education Act,
R.S.O. 1990, c. E.2. The amendments in
issue may generally be described as the new “funding model”. The amendments
bring about fundamental changes in the governance and funding of education in
the province.
Bill 160
places significant limitations upon the powers of
local school boards to control their budgets and expenditures. Those powers
have been moved to the executive branch of the provincial government. The
applicants argue that the removal of some of these powers from local school
boards results in a violation of
s. 93(1)
of the
Constitution Act, 1867

(U.K.), 30 and 31 Vict., c. 3.
Section 93
of the
Constitution Act, 1867,

assigns exclusive jurisdiction over education to the province. Accordingly,
the provincial legislature “…has exclusive power to make laws in relation to
education and to establish a system for the management thereof that it deems
suitable to conditions in the province”:
Reference re: Education Act
(Ontario) and Minority Language Education Rights
(1984),
1984 CanLII 1832 (ON CA)
, 47 O.R. (2d) 1 at
p. 43, 10 D.L.R. (4th) 491 (C.A.).
Section 93(1)
imposes limits by
guaranteeing constitutional protection to denominational rights. This
section states in part:

93. In and for each Province the
Legislature may exclusively make Laws in relation to Education, subject and
according to the following Provisions:—

(1) Nothing in any such Law shall
prejudicially affect any Right or Privilege with respect to Denominational
Schools which any Class of Persons have by Law in the Province at the Union:

The Parties

Application in Court File No. 97-CV-137668

[
2
]

There are two applications before the Court. The first is in Court
File No. 97-CV-137668. The applicant Ontario English Catholic Teachers’
Association (“OECTA”) represents some 32,000 separate school teachers. The
applicants Marshall Jarvis and Claire Ross are separate school teachers. The
applicant Annemarie Ross is a separate school supporter. For ease of reference,
this first application can be referred to as the “OECTA application” or
“separate schools application”.

[
3
]

The intervenor, Ontario Catholic School Trustees’ Association
(“OCSTA”) represents the 29 English-language separate district school boards in
Ontario. The intervenor,
Association Franco-Ontarienne Des Conseils Scolaires Catholiques (“AFOCSC”)
represents French‑language separate school trustees. These intervenors
support the position taken by the respondent, the Attorney General of Ontario
(“Attorney General” or “Government”), that
Bill 160
is constitutionally
and otherwise valid legislation.

Application in Court File No, 98-CV-139317

[
4
]

The second application is in Court File No. 98-CV-139317. The
applicant Ontario Public School Boards’ Association (“OPSBA”) represents over
90 public school boards serving some 1.7 million students. The Metropolitan
Toronto School Board, an applicant in the first instance, existed prior to
January 1998 with the function of making the financial resources of the whole
Metropolitan region available to the Area Boards in each of the municipalities
constituting the former Metropolitan Toronto (now, since the so-called
“megacity” amalgamation, being the “City of Toronto”). The Metropolitan Toronto
School Board was amalgamated into a new entity, the Toronto District School
Board, in January 1998 (formerly the six English-language Metropolitan Area
Boards, including the “Metropolitan Toronto School Board”).

[
5
]

The applicant Wellington County Board of Education, also an
applicant in the first instance, amalgamated into the Upper Grand District
School Board in January 1998, was responsible for public schools in Wellington County.
The Toronto District School Board and Upper Grand District School Board were
added, on consent, as applicants, in replacement of the predecessor
Metropolitan Toronto School Board and Wellington County Board of Education.

[
6
]

The applicant Ontario Secondary School Teachers’ Federation
(“OSSTF”) represents some 35,000 secondary school teachers in the public school
system. As well, OSSTF is the bargaining agent for a number of non-teaching
employees of both public and separate school boards. The applicant Federation
of Women Teachers’ Associations of Ontario (“FWTAO”) represents some 41,000
female elementary teachers in the public school system. The applicant Ontario
Public Teachers’ Federation (“OPTF”) represents 13,000 men who are elementary
school teachers in the public school system. The applicants Robert Churchill
and Elizabeth Sandals are public school supporters. The applicants David
Edwards and Joleene Kemp are separate school supporters.

[
7
]

For ease of reference, this second application before the Court can
be referred to as the “OPSBA application” or the “public schools application”.

[
8
]

The intervenor, Association Des Conseillers (ères) Des Écoles
Publiques De L’Ontario (“ACEPO”) is an association of French-language trustees
representing Ontario’s four
French‑language public district school boards. This intervenor supports
the position of the respondent, the Government. The intervenor Annie Kidder
heads an association known as People for Education First, and supports the
position of the applicants in this application.

[
9
]

The intervenors (other than Annie Kidder) took on a major role in
submissions in support of the Government and in opposition to the applicants.
Accordingly, for case of reference, I refer to the intervenors (other than
Annie Kidder) and the Government collectively as “the respondents”.

The Issues

Introduction

[
10
]

Due to a coincidence of facts and issues, the
OECTA application involving the separate school system was heard in conjunction
with the OPSBA application involving the public school system. Joint
submissions were made and each applicant was supportive of the co‑applicants.
However, the issues raised by the two applications are not identical.

OECTA Application

[
11
]

OECTA applies for a declaration that various
parts of the
Bill 160
are unconstitutional in that they affect
denominational education rights contrary to
s. 93
of the
Constitution
Act, 1867
.
In the alternative, OECTA seeks a declaration that parts of
Bill
160
are contrary to the rule of law.

OPSBA Application

[
12
]

OPSBA submits that
Bill 160
contravenes

s. 93
of the
Constitution Act, 1867

as it affects the public school
system. In the alternative, OPSBA submits that
Bill 160
violates
constitutional convention, fundamental constitutional principles including the
rule of law, and the constitutional principle of “no taxation without
representation”.

The Issues raised by the two Applications

[
13
]

There are six issues raised by the two
applications taken together, being:

(1) Do the provisions of
Bill 160
and
the Funding Model prejudicially affect any right or privilege held by the Roman
Catholic community with respect to denominational schools under
s. 93
of
the
Constitution Act, 1867
?

(2) Are the provisions of
Bill 160
that
relate to the supervision of Boards’ financial affairs and provide for vesting
orders unconstitutional?

(3) Do the provisions of
Bill 160
contravene

s. 93(1)
of the
Constitution Act, 1867

as it applies to public
schools and the public school system?

(4) If the provisions of
Bill 160
do
not contravene
s. 93(1)
of the
Constitution Act, 1867
,
do the
provisions of
Bill 160,
which take away the powers of school boards to
determine and levy property tax rates for school purposes, nonetheless
contravene constitutional convention?

(5) Are the provisions of
Bill 160,
which
confer upon the executive branch of government legislative powers with respect
to education, unconstitutional in that they violate and undermine the “rule of
law” and the principle of effective representation through responsible taxation?

(6) Is
Bill 160
unconstitutional in
conferring upon the Minister of Finance powers with respect to taxation,
including the power to determine the amount thereof free from legislative
scrutiny, debate and approval, without the submission of a “Money Bill”, thus
constituting “taxation without representation”, contrary to sections 53
and 54 and the Preamble of the
Constitution Act, 1867
?

Background to the Legal Issues

[
14
]

Underlying the legal dispute in the case at hand
is, of course, the fact of a significant new policy direction by the provincial
government in respect of the funding of education in Ontario. The submissions were extensive in respect of the changes in
policy. It is necessary to put the legal dispute in context by referring to the
policy underlying the new funding model seen in
Bill 160.
However, this
review serves only to place the issues in context. It is, of course, for the
government alone, and not for the Court, to decide upon education policy. The
Court’s role is limited simply to making a determination and ruling in respect
of the legal issues.

[
15
]

For more than 150 years, until
Bill 160,
locally
elected school trustees, acting collectively as school boards, had the legal
power to supplement provincial education grants through local property tax
levies. The perceived need to have such power to supplement central funding was
twofold. First, communities could respond to local educational priorities
without compromising other areas of expenditure. Second, some communities were
seen to have unusually high costs in delivering a basic level of education.
School boards could go to the local tax base to make up shortfalls in revenue
because of exceptional needs or to meet high costs.

[
16
]

With
Bill 160,
the central provincial
Government now exclusively controls all school board revenues and, hence, it
exclusively funds the separate and public school systems. By new
s. 234
of
the
Education Act
,
the Government provides grants out of general
revenues for educational purposes. By new s. 257.12, the Government raises
property taxes by the establishment of provincial tax rates. (By s. 257.7
the property taxes are levied and collected by the municipalities or by the
district school boards in areas without municipal organization.) These two
components now compromise the totality of the source of public funding of
elementary and secondary education of public and separate schools in Ontario.

[
17
]

The applicants are concerned that the grants
from the provincial Government are insufficient to cover the real costs and
meet the real needs of local schools. A failure to meet this requirement would
mean that the educational services needed by children would not be in place.
The local school boards cannot tax for the balance necessary. Ratepayers cannot
supplement provincial government contributions towards education.

[
18
]

The Government’s answer to these concerns is,
essentially, to trust the Government that the central funding system will be
such that it looks after the needs of Ontario’s students better than the old system. This may or may not be so.
Only time will tell, and the situation may well change over time and with
different governments administering the system. The evidence adduced by the
applicants does, however, at the very least, raise a serious issue as to
whether the Government’s confidence in its assessment of the situation is
misplaced.

[
19
]

The record before the Court suggests that the
funding model has been implemented with haste and without sufficient analysis
as to what the funding arrangements will mean for the quality of education in
the province. The Government’s funding model is based upon expenditure data
garnered through a so-called “Costing Framework” process. The reliability of
the data has been questioned by the advisory Expert Panels appointed by the
Government. There is a mechanical re-allocation of resources. In terms of the
allocation of property tax and provincial grant revenues (being all of the
monies to fund the educational system) the new funding model shifts resources
from assessment rich to assessment poor boards. There is, in effect, a
substantial redistribution of monies. There is an assumption that every
assessment‑rich board can afford to lose some of its previous funding and
still meet the needs of its students. At the same time, there is an assumption
that the amount transferred to each and every assessment poor board will be
sufficient to rectify preexisting shortfalls. It is questionable whether
allowance has been made for the possibility that all relevant needs will not be
met by this mechanical re-allocation of resources.

[
20
]

Some examples of concerns were offered by the
applicants. The major component of the per pupil Foundation Grant is in respect
of classroom teacher salaries. A notional salary is attributed for each teacher
of $50,000.00. In fact, this benchmark is lower than the average salary at the
50th percentile. The costs of specific boards will vary significantly depending
upon the level of experience and the extent of qualifications held by the
teaching staffs. For many boards, the actual teacher salary grids (which
reflect real costs) are higher than the notional average salary grid used in
the new funding model. For example, the applicant Toronto District School Board
estimates the variance between its teachers grid and the so-called “provincial
average grid” to be about $6.9 million annually.

[
21
]

Many of such boards within this category will
only be able to stay within their Foundation Grant allocation for classroom
teachers by securing a reduction in their collective agreement salary grids and
perhaps having to invoke a lockout of teachers to live within the allocation.
Boards cannot reduce their classroom teaching complement below the ratios used
in the Foundation Grant because that would violate the class size provisions of

Bill 160.
Boards which cannot force their classroom teachers to accept
cuts in their compensation packages will have to cannibalize other budget lines
to meet classroom teaching costs. This approach leads to fewer resources being
available to students in boards with above-average classroom teaching costs.

[
22
]

The applicants submit that the data utilized for
the inputs to determine the Foundation Grant in respect of such fundamental
matters as classroom supplies, computer technology and textbooks are
inadequate. The applicant Toronto District School Board submits that its
Foundation Grant allocations will, over three years, result in reductions of
30% in funds available for texts and supplies, and in the order of 40% in
respect of computers. The formula ignores projected enrolment growth and
inflation. Boards are in effect being made to choose, for example, to use their
“Early Learning Grant” to fund junior kindergarten or to enhance programs in
grades 1 to 3. For a board like the Toronto District School Board, junior
kindergarten is considered particularly purposeful to “level the playing field”
for children of inner-city communities. Previously, where government grants
were insufficient to level the playing field, school boards could supplement
these funds through local taxation.

[
23
]

The applicants take the position that the
funding model is inadequate, in both a quantitative as well as a qualitative
sense. OECTA submits that separate school supporters historically never
intended, in the course of their securing constitutional rights at Confederation,
that it would suffice for both the separate and the public school systems to be
treated equally in the manner of funding, albeit both being underfunded.
Rather, OECTA characterizes the historical struggle as securing the fundamental
right for Roman Catholics through s. 93(1) to have the management and
control of the separate school system. Catholics sought to have control reside
with their community rather than with the provincial government. The central
government, seen as reflective of the Protestant majority in the province,
could not be counted upon to understand and be sensitive to the aspirations of
the Roman Catholic minority. Thus, by OECTA’s characterization, the historical
regime contemplated a form of partnership of shared responsibility between the
school boards representing the Catholic population and the provincial
government.

[
24
]

The applicants submit that the essence of
Bill
160
is that it is designed to assist in implementing the fiscal goals of
the current government. The applicants submit that
Bill 160
represents a
revolutionary departure from the historic norms.
Bill 160
removes the
right of school boards to tax, dictates the amount of the expenditures each
board can make in a year, and stipulates by and large how the budget may be
spent. The applicants submit the school boards are now mere conduits of
provincial government policy whose function will largely be to take the brunt
of the criticism from citizens increasingly dissatisfied with the inadequacies
of the educational system due to the constraints on funding.

[
25
]

The Government’s stated objectives through
Bill
160
are to promote and enhance the quality of education, accountability,
efficiency and equality of opportunity for every student in Ontario. The Government submits that the
wide disparity of revenues available on a per pupil basis from school board to
school board in the province was the foremost problem.

[
26
]

“Equality of educational opportunity” is seen as
an important core value to Ontario’s education system by all participants in these applications.
Equality of educational opportunity requires funding. The respondents submit
that
Bill 160
achieves equality of educational opportunity in Ontario. There have historically been wide
disparities in the assessment wealth level of school boards. Any financing
system that relies
significantly
upon local taxation is problematic
because of the unequal distribution of local assessment across Ontario. In the estimation of the
applicants, however, the Government has overstepped the mark and, in so doing,
created new problems without solving old ones.

[
27
]

Under the old funding model all boards were
guaranteed a minimum per pupil level of funding; higher grants were given to assessment-poor
boards to provide for partial equalization of the differences in assessment
wealth. However, according to the applicants, the refusal of provincial
governments to fund to a purportedly adequate level out of general revenues
meant that school boards have had to tax to a significant degree at the local
level. Given the disparities in the local assessment bases, this has meant
differences in funding for education across the province.

[
28
]

Some public school boards, particularly in rural
Ontario, have been unable to
impose a tax, or mill, rate beyond a certain level, given the low level of
wealth of the assessment base. Similarly, separate school boards have generally
had a smaller and less wealthy assessment base than their coterminous public
school boards.

[
29
]

Another aspect of the complex funding dilemmas
has been that the fiscal autonomy of separate boards has been somewhat illusory
in reality. As a practical matter, a separate school board was limited in the
mill rate it could impose by that set by the coterminous public board.
Experience has shown that a separate board cannot tax at a higher rate than the
coterminous public school board or the separate school board will lose some of
its supporters to the public school system, and its tax base will erode.
Therefore, in reality, the separate boards have been captive to the taxing
decisions of their coterminous public school boards.

[
30
]

The overall result has been that there was
generally less money to spend per pupil for school boards in the rural areas
than in the urban centres and, generally, less money for separate school boards
as compared to coterminous public school boards. In contrast, in some urban
centres (in particular, Toronto) with a relatively wealthy assessment base, the
revenues from the property tax resulted in funds in excess of the minimum per
pupil level set by the provincial government. In such instances, grants were
not paid to these school boards by the provincial government, but the boards
could retain the excess funds generated by the local tax levy in excess of the
minimum per pupil level of funding.

[
31
]

Neither side really disagrees with the fact of
the existence of differing assessment bases and the issues arising therefrom.
Where the disagreement so manifestly arises is on the choice of remedy. The
Government has addressed the problem by introducing, through
Bill 160,
a
principle of equal access to revenues by public and separate school boards
through a system of equalization of per pupil funding, with the level of
revenue being controlled and capped by the provincial government. This, in
turn, necessitated an increase in the funding of education from the general
revenues of the province. Some $2.5 billion has been shifted from being taxed
locally by school boards to being paid out of general revenues. (The freed-up
property tax room was then utilized by the municipalities because of the
downloading of the cost of municipal services by the provincial government to
the municipalities.)

[
32
]

The Government could, of course, have made the
changes seen in
Bill 160
without preventing local school boards from
levying local taxes as a top-up to meet perceived local needs. If one takes the
assertions of the Government at face value that all boards now have
adequate

funding through the new funding model then it follows that local boards are
unlikely to want to impose local taxes or, if they do, it is improbable that
the local electorates will respond positively. However, in effectuating
redistribution through
Bill 160
to some boards, the Government has
reduced the present revenues and budgets of other school boards. The Government
is, in effect, stating to this latter group of boards that they are either
inefficient or are overspending in relation to their locally perceived needs as
now determined by the central government. The respondents also submit that it
would be inequitable to allow some communities (in effect, generally urban
communities with their, relatively wealthy assessment bases) to offer their
children greater opportunities in education than those available to children in
other (generally rural) communities because those latter communities are
unable, from a practical standpoint, to raise more monies at the local level.

[
33
]

I do not intend to deal at length with the
considerable submissions made in respect of those school boards whose budgets
decrease by the new funding formula. The submissions as to the adequacy of the
new funding formula are properly left to the political arena. It is enough to
say that the applicants raise serious and meaningful concerns in respect of the
financial limitations and impacts of the model.

[
34
]

By the Government’s figures the total operating
revenue for the Toronto District School Board will fall 0.9% in 1998/99 and by
a total of 5.7% by 2000/01. These figures make no allowance for enrolment
growth (projected at an annual rate of 2.31%), they do not take into account
inflation, and they exclude any consideration of non-operating needs. More
significantly, the Government’s figures for operating revenues also include
more than $600 million as being for transitional mitigation. If this item is to
be ultimately discontinued, as is certainly implied by the Government’s
materials, the cuts to the Toronto District School Board will be even more
drastic, as this transitional quantum of $600 million represents about 11 % of
the total operating revenue grants for the three-year period to 2000/01. This
would bring a total drop in annual operating revenues for the Toronto District
School Board by the fourth year of almost 17%, and even this projection ignores
the impact of enrolment increases and inflation.

[
35
]

The prohibition through the new funding model
upon school boards being able to raise any revenues at all by local property
taxes runs counter to the countless studies done in respect of financing the Ontario education system. See generally,
Ontario,
Report of the Royal Commission on Education
(Toronto: Baptist
Johnston, 1950) at 712, 723; Ontario,
Committee on Taxation Report,
(Ottawa:
Queen’s Printer, 1967) at 406, 408; Ontario,
Report of the Commission on the
Financing of Elementary and Secondary Education
(Toronto: The Commission,
December 1985) at 44, 49, 52;
Toward Education Finance Reform: a Description
of the Present Education Funding Model and the Terms for Reform and the 1992
General Legislative Grants Regulations
(Toronto: Ministry of Education,
1992) at 9; Ontario,
Report of the Ontario Fair Tax Commission,
(Toronto:
University of Toronto Press, 1993) at 677, 681-683; Ontario,
Report of the
Royal Commission on Learning—A Short Version
(Toronto: The Commission,
1994) at 38;
New Foundations for Education Finance: Building on Progress
(Toronto:
Ministry of Education, 1995) at 6; Ontario,
Report of the Working Group on
Education Finance Reform,
(Toronto: Working Group on Education Finance
Reform, 1996); Ontario,
Report of the Education Sub-Panel
(Toronto: Who
Does What Panel and Education Sub-Panel, 1996) at 2, 7.

[
36
]

A central theme in these reports is the need for
tax fairness through the provincial government increasing grants from general
revenues for education to meet the basic needs of the educational system.
However, there is also a generally held view that there is a need for some
local autonomy and flexibility and that the ability to tax locally is a
necessary means to achieving this objective. The purpose of the local levy is
seen as enabling school boards to meet student needs that cannot be met in the
overall funding formula. Educational equity is viewed as not implying simply
that there be equal funding on a per student basis. Rather, equity is seen from
a broader perspective. First, equity mandates a provincially supported
adequate

level of core funding through an overall funding formula. Second, equity
requires unequal funding in ways that are consistent with the different cost
environments and differing educational needs of diverse student populations.
Therefore, while there is a generally held view that there should be a
significant reduction in the reliance upon residential property taxes as a
source of funding, it is important to leave the ability with school boards to
provide for local enrichment in education. Some proposals would limit school
boards in their ability to tax locally to a percentage, say 5% or 10%, of the
school board’s budget. As well, at least one proposal was that local autonomy
be achieved through a special education surcharge tax on personal income rather
than the traditional property tax; see
Report of the Commission on the
Financing of Elementary and Secondary Education in Ontario
at 44, 45, 48,
49. Greater equity is achieved through the income tax which is based upon the
actual increase in the economic power of the taxpayer over the taxation year
rather than a property tax upon presumed but unrealized wealth.

[
37
]

Briefly put, the background to the present
applications may be stated as follows. The present Government has introduced
wide-ranging changes to the financing structure of the educational system.
There is far greater centralization of control than has ever been seen in Ontario to date. In particular, the
amendments remove almost any ability on the pan of local boards to raise
revenues beyond those deemed necessary to them by the provincial government.
Effectively, the government has introduced a monolithic structure into
education governance, based in significant part on centralized command and
control. These changes have provoked furious and searing criticism from a
broadly based spectrum of interests. These criticisms appear on the record
before the Court to have a certain degree of validity. Nevertheless, while
there may be serious and real policy disputes present, it is not this Court’s
function to address them beyond the recognition that it is these disputes which
underlie the present applications. Accordingly, it is to this Court’s role I
now turn, namely the determination of the six legal issues raised by the
applicants.

Issue #1

Do the provisions of Bill 160 and the Funding
Model prejudicially affect any right or privilege held by the Roman Catholic
community with respect to denominational schools under
s. 93
of the

Constitution Act, 1867
?

Position of the Applicants

[
38
]

The applicants submit there are a bundle of
rights and privileges guaranteed by s. 93(1). This provision qualifies the
otherwise plenary power of the provincial legislature in respect of education.
Not all of the rights and privileges guaranteed by
s. 93(1)
are affected
by
Bill 160.
For example, the right to proportional funding is
maintained by
Bill 160
; see
s. 234
of the
Education Act
.
The
applicants submit that the right to tax, the right to determine the level of
expenditures from the funds that would be raised through taxation by the school
board, and the right to prioritize expenditures in respect of monies raised
through such taxation, have all been removed by
Bill 160.
OECTA submits
that these removed rights constitute the ability to manage and control the
separate school system by local separate school boards. OECTA states that the
power to manage and control a separate school system was the essence of the
1867 compromise inherent to the bargain struck at Confederation and guaranteed
through the protection afforded by the exception seen in
s. 93(1)
.

Position of the Respondents

[
39
]

The respondents assert that
Bill 160
and,
in particular, the new funding model implemented thereby, is constitutionally
valid legislation. The respondents claim that
Bill 160
is enacted within
the authority and plenary power of the legislature under
s. 93
of the
Constitution
Act, 1867
.
The respondents submit that because
Bill 160
guarantees
functional equality to the separate school system, the changes it brings,
including the removal of the taxing power from separate school boards, are not
unconstitutional.

Analysis

General Principles of Interpretation

[
40
]

The standard criteria of a s. 93 analysis
have recently been applied by Mr. Justice Sharpe, in
Daly v. Ontario

(
Attorney General
),
1997 CanLII 12210 (ON CTGD)
, [1997] O.J. No. 5040 (QL) (Gen. Div.) at
para.
34
[reported 154 D.L.R. (4th) 464], using the test set forth in the
decision of Chouinard J. in
Attorney General of Quebec v. Greater Hull
School Board

, 15 D.L.R. (4th) 651 (S.C.C.) (“

at 657:

In order to claim the protection of this

(a) There must be a right or privilege

(b) enjoyed by a particular class of

(c) by law;

(d) in effect at the time of the Union;

To this basic approach, one must then add the

First, at 42-43, she sets out the historical perspective through which

The protection of minority religious rights
was a major preoccupation during the negotiations leading to Confederation
because of the perceived danger of leaving the religious minorities in both
Canada East and Canada West at the mercy of overwhelming majorities.

…

The compromise or, as Duff C.J.C. in the
Reference
re Adoption Act, etc.,
1938 CanLII 2 (SCC)
, [1938] 3 D.L.R. 497 at p. 498, [1938] S.C.R.
398 at p. 402, 71 C.C.C. 75, termed it “the basic compact of

[
42
]

The effect of the historical context on the

While due regard must be paid not to give a
provision which reflects a political compromise too wide an interpretation, it
must still be open to the court to breathe life into a compromise that is
clearly expressed.

[
43
]

While the purposive approach set out in the
Bill
30 Reference
is accepted, the Supreme Court has since cautioned against an
overly vigorous application thereof with respect to

Greater

Montreal

Protestant School Board v.
Quebec
(Attorney-General)
(1989),
1989 CanLII 125 (SCC)
, 57 D.L.R.
(4th) 521 (S.C.C.) at 535 (“GMPSB”), Beetz J. observed:

As a constitutional text,
s. 93(1)
may
deserve a “purposive” interpretation but, in so doing, courts must not improperly
amplify the provision’s purpose. While it may be rooted in notions of tolerance
and diversity, the exception in
s. 93
is not a blanket affirmation of
freedom of religion or freedom of conscience. The entrenched right of specified
classes of persons in a province to enjoy publicly sponsored denominational
schools based on a fixed statutory benchmark should not be construed as a
Charter human right or freedom or, to use the expression of Professor Peter
Hogg, a “small bill of rights for the protection of minority religious groups”…

[
44
]

The hallmark of this restricted purposive
approach appears to be flexibility. The cases have been quick to caution that
while 1867 is the touchstone for the delineation of the s. 93 rights,
these rights should not be treated as being frozen in time. The manner in which
the rights may be exercised evolves, and the interpreter must give some
importance to the modern context. This principle has been understood for a long
time and is admirably recited in the judgment of Meredith C.J.C.P. in
Ottawa
Separate School Trustees v. City of Ottawa
(1915),
1915 CanLII 495 (ON SCHCD)
, 24 D.L.R. 497 (Ont.
S.C.) at 501-2:

The right and privilege which the Separate
Schools Act conferred when the Imperial enactment became law, and which the
Separate Schools Acts have ever since conferred, and still confer, was and is a
right to separation, separate public schools of the like character, and
maintained in the like manner, as the general public schools. The machinery may
be altered, the educational methods may be changed, from time to time, to keep
pace with advanced educational systems. It was never meant that the separate
schools, or any other schools, should be left forever in the educational
wilderness of the enactments in force in 1867. Educational methods and machinery
may and must change, but separation, and equal rights regarding public schools,
must remain as long as provincial public schools last, unless the federal or
imperial parliament, which ever may have the power, decrees otherwise.

[
45
]

See also the well known dictum of Viscount Cave in
Hirsch
v. Protestant Board School Commissioners of Montreal,
1928 CanLII 500 (UK JCPC)
, [1928] 1 D.L.R. 1041
(J.C.P.C.) at 1052.

[
46
]

The case law highlights clearly the concept
that, while denominational rights are protected, the province must be granted a
great deal of latitude with regard to its education policies. Without in any
way abandoning the protection of denominational rights, the Court must also be
careful not to impose unnecessary restrictions on the provinces’ plenary powers
to legislate in respect of education.

Pre-Confederation Legislation Relevant to the
Interpretation of
Section 93(1)

[
47
]

Having set out the general approach, the next
step is to consider what rights and privileges existed at the time of
Confederation, which may or may not be encroached upon by Bill 160. In the
years preceding Confederation, the Roman Catholic minority in Ontario pressed for a separate school
system that was not dependent upon the goodwill of the Protestant majority.
There is a progressive evolution of rights for Roman Catholics in Ontario seen
in pre-Confederation legislation, being the Common Schools Act, S.U.C. 1841, c.
18 [Act to repeal certain Acts therein mentioned, and to make further provision
for the establishment and maintenance of Common Schools throughout the Province],
Common Schools Act, S.U.C. 1843, c. 29 [Act for the establishment and
maintenance of Common Schools in Upper Canada], School Act, S.U.C. 1850, c. 48
[Act for the better establishment and maintenance of Common Schools in Upper
Canada], Supplementary School Act, S.U.C. 1853, c. 111, Separate Schools Act,
S.U.C. 1855, c. 131 [Act to amend the laws relating to Separate Schools in
Upper Canada], and Act respecting Separate Schools, C.S.U.C. 1859, c. 65 (the
“Separate Schools Act”) culminating in the Separate Schools Act, S.U.C. 1863
(2nd Sess.), c. 5 [Act to restore to Roman Catholics in Upper Canada certain
rights in respect to Separate Schools] (the “Scott Act”).

[
48
]

There are four statutes that were in force in Upper Canada at the time of Confederation which
are relevant to the interpretation of s. 93(1). They are: the Act
respecting Common Schools in Upper Canada, C.S.U.C. 1859, c. 64 (the “Common
Schools Act”); the Separate Schools Act of 1859; the Scott Act of 1863; and the
Grammar Schools Act, S.U.C. 1865, c. 23 [Act for the improvement of Grammar
Schools in Upper Canada]: see Bill 30 Reference, per Wilson J. at 48-52. The
Separate Schools Act of 1859 conferred the fundamental right to a separate
school system. The Common Schools Act of 1859 and the Scott Act of 1863 are
particularly relevant to the analysis required in the case at hand.

[
49
]

The protection of the minority religious rights
gained through this legislation then became a major focus in the negotiations
that commenced in 1864 and led to Confederation. With Confederation there would
be a separation of the United Province of Canada into Quebec and Ontario. Prior
to Confederation, Catholic separate school rights were gained on the strength
of the Catholic minority in Canada West combining with the Catholic majority in
Canada East.

[
50
]

After Confederation, the two provinces would
have exclusive jurisdiction over education while each would have an isolated
minority religious group. There was a perception of real danger in leaving the
religious minorities in both Canada East and Canada West at the mercy of the
overwhelming majority groups; see
Bill 30 Reference.

The Scott Act of 1863

[
51
]

The
Scott Act
of 1863 guaranteed to
separate school supporters the right to establish separate school boards
managed by elected trustees, the right to levy taxes upon separate school
supporters to meet expenditure needs, and the right to have elected trustees
with the same powers as common school trustees. These powers included the right
to determine the level of expenditures required to support the schools and
ensure their denominational character, the right to be exempt from paying taxes
to support the common school system, and the right to a proportional share of
provincial funding for education within the province.

[
52
]

The Preamble to the
Scott Act
sets forth
the purpose of that legislation. The intent was “to restore” to Roman Catholics
rights formerly enjoyed, and to bring the provisions of the legal regime for
separate schools “more in harmony” with the provisions seen for common (now
called “public”) schools in the
Common Schools Act
of 1859. Section 3
provided for the election of trustees. Section 7 provided to the trustees the
power to levy taxes upon parents sending children or upon separate school
supporters, and to have all the powers of trustees of common schools under the
Common
Schools Act.
By ss. 27, para. 2, 27, para. 10, 27, para 11, 27,
para. 12, 36, 79, para. 12, and 79, para. 18, of that Act,
trustees of common schools could levy property taxes based upon the assessment
roll. Section 27, para. 10 of the
Common Schools Act
of 1859
conferred upon the trustees of common schools (and thus, by operation of
s. 7 of the
Scott Act
upon the trustees of separate schools) an
unqualified power “to assess and cause to be collected an additional rate, in
order to pay the balance of the Teacher’s salary and other expenses of such
school”; see Le Dain J. in
Greater Hull

at 671.

[
53
]

Inherent to the right of a separate school
system is the right of management and control. Public and separate schools are
based upon fundamentally different approaches to education. Public schools see
the separation of secular from religious education as being advantageous. In
contrast, separate school supporters believe that religious instruction and
values should permeate and be integral to the teaching of secular subjects. See
generally Anglin C.J.C. in
Tiny
Separate
School
Trustees v. The King,
1927 CanLII 9 (SCC)
, [1927] S.C.R. 637
at 656, [1927] 4 D.L.R. 857;
Ottawa
Separate
School
Trustees v. The City of
Ottawa

(1916),
1916 CanLII 546 (ON SCAD)
, 30 D.L.R. 770 (Ont. S.C.), per Meredith C.J.O. at 774;
Brophy
v. Attorney-General of
Manitoba
,
[1895] A.C. 202 (J.C.P.C.)
, per the
Lord Chancellor at 214 and
Daly.

[
54
]

The
Scott Act
of 1863 recognized this
right in s. 7 in stating that the trustees of separate schools shall have
all the powers in respect of separate schools that the trustees of common
schools have under the
Common Schools Act
of 1859. Sections 27 and 79 of
the
Common Schools Act
gave extensive powers to the trustees of common
schools: However, the fundamental policy underlying the two school systems was
that power over education was divided between the central authority and the
local, elected trustees. Local self-management by the trustees was considered
to be essential by the architect of the overall school system, the Chief
Superintendent, Dr. Eggerton Ryerson. See
Reference re
Education Act (
Ontario
) and Minority Language
Education Rights

at 42, 48. Part VI of the
Education
Act

sets forth the current duties, powers and responsibilities of all
school boards.

[
55
]

By s. 14 of the
Scott Act
supporters
of separate schools were exempted from the payment of common school rates. By
s. 20 every separate school was entitled to a proportional share in the
funds granted by the legislature for the support of common schools on the basis
of pupils attending. By s. 21 of the
Scott Act
a separate school
was not to share in the monies arising from the local assessment for public
schools.

[
56
]

The
Scott Act
also imposed certain
limitations upon the independent management of separate schools. By s. 26
separate schools were subject to regulations imposed by the Council of Public
Instruction for Upper Canada.
This central authority set the minimum standards and the broad, general policy
for the overall school system. By s. 119, para. 4, of the
Common
Schools Act
the Council could make regulations for the “organization and
discipline of Common Schools”. Section 13 of the
Scott Act
required that
separate school teachers be subject to the same examinations and receive their
certificates of qualifications in the same manner as the common school
teachers. As well, while s. 7 provided that separate school trustees would
have the same powers as the common school trustees, this arguably meant that
when the province expanded or reduced common school trustee powers there would
be a corresponding impact upon the powers of separate school trustees, provided
that any reductions in powers did not prejudicially affect the denominational
aspects of education. The power of separate school trustees in Upper Canada over the curriculum was not
absolute, and the province had an overriding regulatory authority, although no
regulations had been passed at the time of Union; see
GMPSB.

[
57
]

Therefore, Catholic school boards have two
aspects to their duties. They carry out the ordinary responsibilities of
trustees as prescribed in the
Education Act
; see, for example,

ss. 170
to
171
. At the same time, they carry out these duties in a way
that reflects their denominational mandate so as to reflect the interests,
values and aspirations of the Catholic school supporters. Therefore, for
example, they can take into account the religious faith and practices in the
employment of teachers; see for example
Caldwell v. Stuart
(1984),
1984 CanLII 128 (SCC)
, 15
D.L.R. (4th) 1 (S.C.C.), and
Daly.
They can also, for example, adapt
prescribed curricula somewhat, and create additional curricula, to accommodate
denominational needs; see
GMPSB
per

Beetz J. at 546.

The Rights Protected

[
58
]

The relevant “Class of Persons” having
denominational rights in Ontario at Confederation was the entire Roman Catholic
community at large;
Ottawa Separate School Board Trustees v. City of Ottawa
(1916),

1916 CanLII 419 (UK JCPC)
, 32 D.L.R. 10 (J.C.P.C.) at pp. 12-13. The phrase “by Law” refers to any “Right
or Privilege” affirmed by statute, not to mere practices followed by
institutions or officials;
Bill 30 Reference,
at 45. As well, the
Constitution protects not only the ultimate objective of a separate,
denominational education seen in
s. 93(1)
. It also protects the means
necessary to achieve that objective;
GMPSB at 545, 546.

Management and Control

[
59
]

Along with their complaints about the removal of
the taxation power, the applicants have made submissions regarding the method of
delivery of funding. The applicants submit that the spending strictures imposed

unconstitutional interference with the right of management and control of
separate schools.

[
60
]

This submission is rejected. Leaving aside the
issue of the right to tax locally and the possible consequences of the denial
of the right, there is not otherwise any evidence of any prejudicial effect on
a
denominational
right because of the strictures upon the powers of
management imposed by
Bill 160.
Within the constraints of the spending
envelopes for all school boards under
Bill 160,
the separate school
boards retain full managerial discretion. The prescriptive elements of the new
funding model will direct board spending to a considerable degree. However,
there is nothing to suggest that Catholic boards will be prevented from taking
denominational matters into account in all aspects of their operations, such as
teacher hiring, curriculum, programs and in respect of capital facilities.

Right to Tax

[
61
]

The interference with the right of local
taxation is a somewhat more complicated question. The right to tax seen in
s. 7 of the Scott Act remained in provincial legislation until
Bill
160.
Prior to repeal by
Bill 160,
ss. 115(1), 120(1),
250(3)
,
252
of
the
Education Act
allowed a separate school board to set tax rates, levy

(2), (3) and 252 provided a similar scheme for public school boards.)
Bill
160
provides, through new s. 257.12, for the Minister of Finance to
set the tax rates, and s. 257.12 requires the municipality to levy taxes
in accordance with those rates. Division C of the new Part IX has provisions
for “Taxes Set By Boards” which would allow for a continuation of the right of
school boards to tax (although it is noted the Minister of Finance has a broad

for the “varying, limiting or
excluding
” (emphasis added) of the powers
given to municipalities and boards by the Division). However, Division C is
rendered inoperative by s. 257.106 in Division F of
Bill 160.
The
only other provision contained in Division F is s. 257.107 which provides
for a committee to be appointed by the Lieutenant Governor in Council to review
and report by June 30, 2003, as to whether the legislation and regulations
governing education funding operate “in a fair and non-discriminatory manner”
so as to meet the standard set forth in s. 234(2). Perhaps this intended
review is meant to imply that the legislature might respond to the resulting
report by then making Division C operative.

[
62
]

The intervenor OCSTA submits that the
denominational nature of education in Catholic schools is best effected in the
expenditure

decisions of Catholic boards rather than in the way in which they obtain
their monies to fund those expenditures. However, expenditure decisions are
premised upon having monies to fund the desired actions.

[
63
]

The affidavit expert evidence as to the intent
underlying the evolution of the right to tax seen in s. 7 of the
Scott
Act
was in direct conflict. However, upon analysis, the conflict is more
apparent than real. Dr. Robert T. Dixon, who provided affidavit evidence
in support of OCSTA and the Government, emphasizes that separate school
supporters historically were looking for substantial equality with public
schools in terms of powers and finances. He states that he has not found any
record that separate school boards have been concerned about the source of
funds to enable them to gain financial equity. Their concern has been that
adequate funds were available. Dr. Mark G. McGowan, as an expert for the
applicants, states that winning the right to tax was a means to manage and
direct separate schools. He and Professor R.D. Gidney emphasize that separate
school supporters were seeking local autonomy, and that financing was a means
to this end. However, all the experts agree with the obvious. Roman Catholics
sought a separate, Catholic school system with sufficient management and
control over their school system to ensure that Catholic education was realized
within their schools. But such a denominational system cannot operate in a
vacuum. Thus, it was necessary to have the right of adequate financing.

[
64
]

The issue that is thus raised by the new funding
model of
Bill 160
is whether or not the authority to levy rates on
taxpayers as a means of financing must necessarily be maintained in legislation
because of the constitutional guarantee seen in s. 93(1).

The Issue as to the
“
Denominational Aspects
”
Analysis

[
65
]

At the beginning of this analysis, I touched on
the general principles of interpretation of section 93(1). I did not,
however, deal with the question of denominational versus non‑denominational
at that point. This issue is important to this application, and is most
conveniently dealt with now.

[
66
]

The Government submits it has the constitutional
power to legislate to remove the non‑denominational component of levying
taxes when such removal is done within the overall context of
Bill 160.
The
Government submits that the Supreme Court of Canada has adopted an approach
referred to as an “aspect analysis” beginning with
GMPSB
in 1989. The
Government in the case at hand argues that the right to levy property taxes is
not necessary to give effect to denominational guarantees in Ontario. Rather, it is simply funding, by
whatever means, that is required. The Government submits that there is now
proportional funding on a per pupil basis in respect of all funds provided to
the overall school system in Ontario. As well, the Government submits, there is the strong probability
from a practical standpoint that the provincial electorate will always insist
upon adequate funding for public schools by the provincial government, thereby
automatically assuring adequate funding to the separate school system as its
financing is tied by
Bill 160
to that available to public schools.

[
67
]

The Government submits that the “aspect”
approach introduces a disciplined process when determining whether a particular
legislative or regulatory measure is unconstitutional as prejudicially
affecting a denominational right or privilege. That is, the Government asserts
that a power which in itself is conceptually non-denominational in nature, such
as financing through the right to tax, must be shown to be necessary to support
intrinsic denominational rights or privileges. Financing is just a means to an
end. The Government submits that unless actual or inevitable prejudice is
established because of the Government’s amendments to eliminate the right to
tax through
Bill 160
(while at the same time ensuring finding
proportionally on a per pupil basis) that the amendments are constitutionally
valid. The Government says the correct question is whether the continued right
of the separate school boards to levy property taxes is necessary to assure the
protection of the denominational character of separate schools. The
respondents, in essence, submit that financing is a protected
non-denominational aspect of denominational schools but local taxation is not a
necessary element to give effect to denominational guarantees.

“
Aspect
”
Jurisprudence

[
68
]

As noted,
GMPSB
is the formal beginning
of the “aspect” analysis. In
GMPSB
, the Supreme Court considered
regulations by the Quebec
government which had the purpose of establishing a uniform curriculum in schools
throughout the province. However, the regulations did not set the content of
religious and moral instruction in denominational schools, but left this to the
Protestant or Catholic committee of the Conseil supérieur de l’Education, an
administrative body established by statute. The appellants contended that the
regulations were
ultra vires
the province because they violated claimed
rights under
s. 93(1)
which enabled the Protestant minority in Quebec to manage and control its own
schools and to regulate, subject to provincial rules of general application,
the curriculum of study.

[
69
]

Under the
Act respecting Provincial Aid for
Superior Education,—and
Normal
and Common Schools,
C.S.L.C. 1861, c.
15 (the “7867
Act
”), the authority over schools was divided between a
government-appointed Council of Public Instruction and school commissioners and
trustees who represented the local community. The rights and privileges
accorded with respect to denominational schools in Quebec by the
1861 Act
are guaranteed by
s. 93(1)
of the
Constitution
Act, 1867
.
Thus, the 1861 Act operates as one standard for denominational
rights in Quebec as does the
Scott
Act
of 1863 in Ontario.

[
70
]

Section 93(2)
of the
Constitution Act, 1867

is
also relevant to any consideration of protected denominational rights in Quebec.
Section 93(2)
states that:

93(2) All the Powers, Privileges, and
Duties at the Union by Law
conferred and imposed in Upper Canada on the Separate
Schools and School Trustees of the Queen’s Roman Catholic Subjects shall be and
the same are hereby extended to the Dissentient Schools of the Queen’s
Protestant and Roman Catholic Subjects in Quebec:

[
71
]

Beetz J., with McIntyre, Lamer and La Forest JJ. concurring, in
GMPSB,
held
that the regulations were within the provincial authority yet met the
requirements of the constitutional guarantees in
s. 93(1)
. The
non-denominational aspects of the curriculum affected by the regulations were
not in respect of denominational guarantees. By leaving the denominational
content of the curriculum with the Protestant committee of the Conseil, the Quebec government had conformed to
s. 65(2) of the
1861
Act which gave to the curé, priest or minister
the exclusive right of selection in respect of books having reference to
religion and morals in denominational schools.

[
72
]

The respondents rely upon the statements of
Beetz J. He stated, at 536, that in interpreting the phrase “with respect to

s. 93(1)

are those necessary to give effect to denominational guarantees.

[
73
]

at 553, that she reached the same result as Beetz J. She noted at 553, 554,

though no regulations had been passed at the time of Union.
Section 93(2)
of
the
Constitution Act, 1867

was meant to enhance the constitutional
protection otherwise accorded to dissentient schools in Quebec (through
s. 93(1)

their position with the separate schools in Ontario. Therefore, as in Ontario, it is open to the legislature in Quebec to regulate the powers of all schools, including dissentient

However, Wilson. J. made a
qualification to the “non-denominational aspects” approach of Beetz J. Wilson

It would be my view that
all
powers,
privileges and duties conferred or imposed on separate schools in Ontario at

s. 93(2)
to dissentient schools in Quebec and have the constitutional
protection of
s. 93(1)
.
This is so because, in my view, the words
“
with
respect to Denominational Schools
”
in
s. 93(1)
do not contain the
internal limitation imparted into those words by my colleague.

reason, in my view, why the dissentient schools in Quebec do not have, by
virtue of the extension in
s. 93(2)

s. 93(1)
for the substantial measure of control over curriculum which the

[
74
]

of the province of Ontario was limited and did not extend to those aspects of the curriculum
necessary for the maintenance and preservation of the denominational character

Public School Boards’ Assn.
v.
Alberta

(Attorney General),
1998 ABCA 94 (CanLII)
, [1998] A.J. No. 317 (QL) (C.A.), per Berger J.A. [now reported as

Alberta
v.
Alberta
(Attorney General)

(1998), 158 D.L.R.
(4th) 267, 78 A.C.W.S. (3d) 933 (Alta. C.A.)].

[
75
]

The wording of section 93(1) reads “Right
or Privilege
with respect
to Denominational Schools” (emphasis added).

in Quebec. As such, the “denominational aspects” analysis

with

Bill 160.

[
76

per

[

The application of the

Hull

The plaintiffs in that case sought a

1979
(Que.), c. 72 were unconstitutional as contravening

of the

Act, 1867

[
78

in particular, ss. 73 and 74, stating:

[T]he classes of persons in question
enjoyed the right to have their denominational schools managed by school

and
(2)
of the
Constitution Act, 1867

Section 93(1)

1861 Act

[
83
]

[
84
]

The
1861 Act
created two school systems
in each of the cities of Montreal and Quebec, one

1861 Act

[W]hat matters is having the financial and
physical resources to operate school boards. The taxing power is only one
possible means of attaining this end. If it can be done otherwise, such as by

[
85
]

The Government argues that this statement lends
further support to its position that provincial legislation can remove the
taxing power so long as there is a non-discriminatory approach in funding as
between the public and separate school systems. The Government submits that the
taxing power is not a right which falls within the category of there being a

per se
prejudicial effect upon its removal.

[
86
]

The applicants submit that the statement is
obiter,

and that the Court did not qualify its findings in
Attorney General of
Quebec
v. Greater
Hull
School
Board.
Indeed, Gonthier J. approved, at
285, 286, of the Supreme Court’s conclusion in
Greater Hull

that:

…the right conferred on commissioners and
trustees to receive grants on a proportional basis
and
the right to levy
taxes within the boundaries of their respective municipalities are
rights
with
respect to denominational schools, and so protected by s. 93(1) of the
Constitution. [Emphasis added.]

[
87
]

In
Ontario Home Builders’ Assn. v.
York
Region. Board of Education
(1996),
1996 CanLII 164 (SCC)
, 137 D.L.R. (4th) 449 (S.C.C.) (“
OHBA
”), the Supreme
Court considered Part III of the
Development Charges Act,
R.S.O. 1990,
c. D.9
. Under this legislation a school board could raise funds for new school
construction on land being developed for residential or commercial purposes, by
means of development charges imposed on the land. The proceeds from an
education development charge levied by a board by-law are payable to the
municipality by the developer, with the proceeds not being identified by school
support. The monies raised under the by-law of one school board are used to build

recovering the financial resources needed on a per pupil basis to construct
schools in areas of new growth.

[
88
]

A public and a separate board each passed
by-laws imposing education development charges. The legislation made no
distinction between public and separate school boards or as between their
supporters. The appellant sought to have the by-laws quashed.

[
89
]

One issue considered was whether
s. 93(1) rights were prejudicially affected. In
OHBA
, Iacobucci J.
held
that the principle of proportionality in s. 20 of the
Scott Act
was
in reality “…the means to a constitutional end which is equality of educational
opportunity” (at 489). The substantive purpose underlying s. 20 was the
achievement of an educational system that distributes provincial funds in “a
fair and non-discriminatory manner to common and separate schools alike” (at
490). The principle of proportionality seen in s. 20 of the
Scott Act
was
carried forward in s. 122 of the
Education Act.

[
90
]

Iacobucci J. further held that this statutory
provision governed the
Development Charges Act
which honoured the
obligation for a fair and non-discriminatory distribution. Iacobucci J. noted
at 489 that education development charges resulted in
