grants to
which s. 20 of the
Scott Act
had never been applied. The principle
of equal per pupil local grants measured annually is not sensibly applied to
capital grants for the purpose of creating assets used over a number of years.
A strict, formalistic application of proportionality would lead to the absurd
situation of requiring the province to fund the construction of an unneeded
separate school merely because the coterminous public school board required and
received a capital grant for a new school (at 489). Indeed, a strict,
formalistic proportionality in the provincial grant system could lead to a
serious inequality of educational opportunity. Hence, historically the province
had paid equalizing grants to school boards only after taking into account
their ability to raise funds on their own through the local assessment base.
Thus, the operating grants paid out to boards varied significantly, reflecting
the disparity in the levels of local assessment wealth.

[
91
]

It is clear from the foregoing case law that the
issue of whether a right is denominational or non-denominational is a necessary
question for a court to ask on any matter involving
s. 93
. This has been
accepted by Justice Sharpe in
Daly
,
and indeed, arguably pre-dates its
formal inception in
GMPSB.
To my mind, cases such as
Board of
Trustees of the Roman Catholic Separate Schools of Belleville v. Grainger
(1878),
25 Gr. 570
,
Ottawa Separate School Trustees v. Mackell
(1916),
1916 CanLII 418 (UK JCPC)
, 32 D.L.R.
1 (J.C.P.C.), and the
Reference re Education Act (Ontario) and Minority
Language Education Rights
reflect an acknowledgment of this point. However,
as the case law also clearly reflects, the inquiry does not end there. There is
still the question of whether the non-denominational right is necessary to
secure a denominational purpose.

Purpose of the Taxation Right

[
92
]

The principle of proportionality referred to in
OHBA

is properly viewed as the means to the constitutional objective of equality
of educational opportunity. However, the objective of equality of educational
opportunity is not the only objective of the separate school system. There are
other core values consistent with the objective of equality of educational
opportunity. In reality, these core values encompass the more fundamental,
underlying value of the freedom to differ and to make autonomous decisions. The
most visible core value is the objective of a
separate
system of
denominational schools. A correlative core value is the ability to have the
financial
means
to make the
expenditure
decisions seen as appropriate by the
local separate school community to achieve the desired degree of autonomy
inherent to a separate denominational school system. The right to tax locally
was historically critical to a viable separate school system because of the
shortfall in provincial grants. However, this does not mean the right to tax
was a limited purpose right which is exhausted once the provincial government
devises a system of proportional funding that is at a level adequate (in the
eyes of the provincial government) to achieve equality of educational
opportunity for the students of the separate and public school systems alike.

[
93
]

Section 7 of the
Scott Act
does not set
any limit in the legal expression of the right to tax. Nor, of course, does
s. 93(1) in giving constitutional protection to the pre-Confederation
right to tax. Financing is a necessary means or aspect to achieving the
objective of a separate, denominational educational system. It is not the
particular form of the tax that is essential. Rather, it is the
independent
right
to finance by raising money by the taxation of
separate
school
supporters that is critical to the prime objective of guaranteeing the autonomy
of a separate, denominational school system. The expression of the right to tax
in pre‑Confederation law through s. 7 of the
Scott Act
as a
stand alone, unqualified right speaks as to its importance. The right to tax
affirmed by s. 7 is separate and apart from the right to proportional
funding accorded by s. 20 of the
Scott Act.
The non-denominational
component of being able to levy a property tax to assist in financing is
affirmed by s. 93(1) as a “Right or Privilege with respect to
Denominational Schools”.

[
94
]

The constitutionally protected right to tax
assures the local separate school community of two complementary objectives.
First, it guarantees the community that it has the inviolable legal right to
ensure an adequate level of funding to achieve the objective of equality of
educational opportunity for its children
as perceived by the community
itself,
taking into account its particular needs. Moreover, this can be
achieved without the restrictions imposed by a narrower perception on the part
of either the legislature, or the provincial education bureaucracy, as to what
is the limit of funding properly appropriate to educate the community’s
children. Second, the right to tax provides the means whereby the separate
school community can meet its perceived needs within the context of its core
value of a
separate, denominational
education.

[
95
]

The rights guaranteed by s. 93(1) include
the right to proportional sharing by separate schools in provincial government
funding for education.
Bill 160
meets this obligation. As well, the Government
has brought a greater quantitative amount of funding to the overall separate
school system through the redistribution scheme inherent to
Bill 160.
In
this sense,
Bill 160
enhances the separate school system at this point
in time by providing more monies to it.

[
96
]

The question is whether this, in itself, is
sufficient to meet the constitutional obligations imposed upon the provincial
government.

[
97
]

In my opinion,
Bill 160
is not sufficient
to meet these constitutional obligations. The Government’s approach makes the
Roman Catholic community hostage to the provincial government as to the
extent

of financing of the separate school system. Theoretically, the provincial
government could slash funding substantially to the point that the Roman
Catholic community held the view that there was inadequate funding in providing
the educational opportunity
sought by them
for their children. However,
so long as there was proportional funding and consequential equality of
educational opportunity with the public system there would be no independent
means to enhance the financial resources of the separate school system.

[
98
]

In my view, the concept of a “separate”
education system implies not only the need for financing but also the need for
a means of financing from within the Roman Catholic community. A “separate
school system” truly responsive to its own religious community of interest is
not one that is captive to a government-imposed ceiling upon its expenditures
through preventing access to local financing. It is true that the likelihood of
the present situation created by
Bill 160
would not be foreseen in
pre-Confederation times. It cannot be said that s. 7 of the
Scott Act
was
designed with this specific, potential problem in contemplation. Rather, the
visible problem being addressed pre-Confederation and to the present has been
the necessity of access to local financing to make up the shortfall in revenues
due to the inadequacy of government grants. This historical problem has been
met by
Bill 160,
at least if one accepts the Government’s position that
there is now to be a quantitative adequacy in the grants paid to school boards
in the province.

[
99
]

Nevertheless, despite the fact that s. 7 of
the
Scott Act
was not designed with the present situation in mind, one
cannot ignore the rather salient fact that s. 7 was created separate and
apart, independent of s. 20. The existence of s. 7 has to mean
something, and to my mind it has to mean that s. 93(1) guarantees an
independent financing mechanism to the Roman Catholic community, supplementary
and complementary to the right of proportionality, but not subsumed within it.
Although, as OCSTA suggests, this independent right may practically be of very
little use, it is still a constitutional right. Constitutional rights are
constitutional rights for a reason; they are guaranteed and protected
notwithstanding that at a given point in time it may not appear that a given
right is necessary or effective. While the Government’s intentions may be
benevolent in regard to the Roman Catholic education community, that cannot
change the fact that the taxation power is constitutionally guaranteed, and it
would ill-behoove this Court to countenance its removal.

[
100
]

There are five certainties. First, there is a denominational right
of Roman Catholics in Ontario
to a separate school system. Second, adequate financing is a necessary means to
the real achievement of that separate school system. Third, the language of
s. 7 of the
Scott Act
in conferring the right to tax locally is
clear and express in providing an independent means to the Roman Catholic
community to achieve the realization of their separate school system. Fourth,
the language of s. 93(1) protects the rights and privileges “with respect
to Denominational Schools” accorded by the law, including s. 7 of the
Scott
Act,
at Confederation. Fifth, the right to tax locally, recognized by
s. 7 of the
Scott Act,
is repealed by
Bill 160.
Constitutional
rights are constitutional rights. In the absence of a constitutional amendment,
the province cannot lawfully impinge upon such rights.

Disposition

[
101
]

The submissions of the applicants with respect to the constitutional
right or privilege of the Roman Catholic community to tax with respect to
denominational schools are accepted. Bill 160, insofar as it removes the
taxation power from the Roman Catholic educational community, is
unconstitutional as a violation of the s. 93(1) guarantee.

Issue # 2

Are the provisions of Bill 160 that relate to
the supervision of Boards’ financial affairs and provide for vesting orders
unconstitutional?

Position of the Applicants

[
102
]

Division D of Part IX of
Bill 160
deals with the “Supervision
of Boards’ Financial Affairs”. The applicants submit that these provisions of
Division D “prejudicially affect separate school supporters’ constitutionally
protected right to exclusive management and control”. The applicants submit
that the provisions of Division D lack both limits and definition.

Position of the Respondents

[
103
]

The Attorney-General submits that the constitutional validity of
Division D does not properly arise in this case because no school boards are
under supervision at the present time and, accordingly, there is no factual
underpinning to support a constitutional challenge. Alternatively, the
Attorney-General submits that Division D is valid because it is time limited,
with readily ascertainable standards for both its imposition and removal.

Analysis

Necessity of Factual Foundation

[
104
]

In support of the argument that the Court should not consider
Division D at this juncture, the respondents point to the jurisprudence of the
Supreme Court mandating a factual foundation before a court can consider the
constitutional validity of legislation; see for instance,
McEvoy v. Attorney
General of New Brunswick
(1983),
1983 CanLII 149 (SCC)
, 148 D.L.R. (3d) 25 (S.C.C.), and
R. v.
Danson
(1990),
1990 CanLII 93 (SCC)
, 73 D.L.R. (4th) 686 (S.C.C.).

[
105
]

The requirement of a factual foundation is, as the Supreme Court has
so clearly held, an important one. Nevertheless, the factual matrix necessary
will, of course, vary from case to case and from issue to issue. In cases where
it is alleged that a state action is prejudicial
per se,
there may be
less need for the requirement of a factual foundation. In the case at hand, I
find that no further evidence than what is presently before the Court is
necessary before the Court is required to consider Division D.

[
106
]

In
Ottawa Separate School Trustees v. Ottawa
(1916),
1916 CanLII 419 (UK JCPC)
, 32
D.L.R. 10 (J.C.P.C.), the Privy Council was concerned with legislation
conferring a right to replace a separate school board with other management. The
legislation in question granted sweeping powers to interfere, subject to very
few discernible standards. The government asserted that the legislation had not
been used, and that there was an onus on the trustees to show prejudice. Given
the sweeping powers granted by the legislation, the Privy Council rejected this
argument at 13:

[I]t is difficult to appreciate the
argument that no legal right or privilege existing in the province at the Union with respect to denominational
schools has been prejudicially affected. It is possible that an interference
with a legal right or privilege may not in all cases imply that such right or
privilege has been prejudicially affected. It is not necessary to consider such
a possibility, and this question does not arise for decision in the appeal. The
case before their Lordships is not that of a mere interference with a right or
privilege, but of a provision which enables it to be withdrawn
in toto
for
an indefinite time. Their Lordships have no doubt that the power so given would
be exercised with wisdom and moderation, but it is the creation of the power
and not its exercise that is subject to objection, and the objection would not
be removed even though the powers conferred were never exercised at all. To
give authority to withdraw a right or privilege under these conditions
necessarily operates to the prejudice of the class of person affected by the
withdrawal. Whether or not a different policy might have been preferable,
either in the opinion of the provincial legislature, or in that of the Courts,
is not a relevant consideration.
It was argued that no evidence on behalf of
the appellant Board had been called to prove that the withdrawal of their
rights, powers, and privileges, operated to their prejudice. In the opinion of
their Lordships no such evidence was necessary.
[Emphasis added.]

[
107
]

While the powers provided by the present
Education Act
may or
may not prejudicially affect s. 93(1) rights in the same manner as in
Ottawa
Separate School Trustees,
it is incumbent on this Court to consider the
issue. The fact that the Privy Council felt it necessary to consider similar
powers (in terms of vesting orders), suggests that while a more specific
factual foundation is important in many cases, it is not a necessity in the
present one.

Protections in Division D

[
108
]

In the consideration of this question, the Privy Council sets the
analytical standard: does the authority to withdraw a right or privilege under
these conditions necessarily operate to the prejudice of the class of persons affected
by the withdrawal?

[
109
]

What then are the conditions set out by the legislation? Section
257.30 provides:

257.30(1) The Minister may direct an
investigation of the financial affairs of a board if,

(
a
)

the financial statements
of the board for a fiscal year, or the auditor’s report on the statements…
indicate that the board had a deficit that year;

(
b
)

the board has failed to
pay any of its debentures or instruments prescribed under clause 247(3)(
f
)
or interest on them, after payment of the debenture instrument or interest is
due and has been demanded;

(c)
the
board has failed to pay any of its other debts or liabilities when due and
default in payment is occasioned from financial difficulties affecting the
board; or

(d)
the
Minister has concerns about the board’s ability to meet its financial
obligations.

[
110
]

Under s. 257.30(2) the Minister may appoint an investigator to
consider the affairs of the board, but under s. 257.30(6) the investigator
may not recommend a vesting order unless there is evidence of financial default
or deficit, or a probability of such. Section 257.31 gives the Minister the
power to give directions to a board regarding its financial affairs, and the
Minister may request a vesting order where the Minister is of the opinion that
the directions of the Minister have not been followed.

[
111
]

The precondition for the imposition of a vesting order is a deficit
or default, or likelihood thereof. It appears that, given the Minister’s power
to make directions, a deficit or default may not be an absolute precondition,
but I am unconcerned by that ambiguity, because the condition for lifting a
vesting order is absolute and not subject to discretion. The order
has
to
be lifted if it is clear that there is no deficit or default. Section 257.50
provides:

257.50(1) The Lieutenant Governor in
Council shall revoke an order made under subsection 257.31 (2) or (3) if
the Lieutenant Governor in Council is of the opinion that the affairs of a
board no longer need to be administered under this Division.

(2) The Lieutenant Governor in Council
shall

revoke an order made under subsection 257.31 (2) or (3) if the
financial statements of a board for a fiscal year and the auditor’s report on
the statements submitted to the Ministry under
section 252
indicate that
the board did not have a deficit for the fiscal year. [Emphasis added.]

[
112
]

The
Act
goes on to reiterate the constitutional protections
provided to separate school supporters in s. 93(1), in s. 257.52:

257.52(1) Nothing in this Division
authorizes the Minister to interfere with or control,

(
a
)

the denominational
aspects of a Roman Catholic board;

…

(2) The powers under this Division shall be
exercised in a manner that is consistent with,

(
a
)

the denominational
aspects of a Roman Catholic board;

[
113
]

Of course this last provision does no more than reiterate a
protected right that the separate school boards already have under
s. 93(1), but, to the extent that it does so, it does make the right
statutorily explicit.

[
114
]

These conditions must then be measured against the standard in
Ottawa
Separate School Trustees,
to determine whether or not they too necessarily
operate “to the prejudice of the class of persons affected by the withdrawal”.
At the heart of the Privy Council’s decision was the determination that the
provisions it was dealing with provided for an indefinite removal of a board,
subject to unclear standards.

[
115
]

In
Re Ottawa Separate Schools
(1917),
1917 CanLII 584 (ON SCAD)
, 41 O.L.R. 259, 40
D.L.R. 465 (S.C.A.D.), the Court of Appeal considered legislation that had been
altered in light of the earlier Privy Council decision. In referring to the
Privy Council decision, Hodgins J.A. summarized what he took to be the ratio of
that case, at 268:

It was, therefore, the
substitution—indefinite in point of time and depending for its cessation upon
the uncontrolled view of a designated Minister—of a nominated Board in place of
the elective body provided for by the original statute, that determined the
case adversely to the Commission.

[
116
]

In the final event, the Court of Appeal found that the new
legislation was acceptable, as it provided more definite standards. Professor
Hogg, in
Constitutional Law of Canada,
4th ed. (Toronto: Carswell, 1997)
(looseleaf) reconciles the cases on this basis, at 54-9:

In the Court’s view, it was the indefinite
and discretionary nature of the suspending power in the first statute which
made it bad. The more limited suspending power in the second statute was good.
A provision calculated only to secure the observance of the law by separate
school trustees was not inconsistent with the trustees’ power of management,
because that power should not be treated as enabling the trustees to conduct
their schools in defiance of the law.

[
117
]

The respondents submit that as the provisions referred to above,
namely the ability to recommend a vesting order only where there is a deficit
or default and the mandatory requirement that the order be lifted in the
absence of a deficit as well as the statutory reiteration of the s. 93(1)
rights, address the concerns of the
Ottawa
cases, the legislation is
valid.

[
118
]

The applicants argue that these safeguards are insufficient to meet
the standard. The applicants point in their factum to three factors they assert
were relied upon as safeguards in
Re Ottawa Separate Schools
:

(i) an order placing a separate school
board under supervision could be made only where the board was neglecting or
refusing to carry out its responsibilities according to law;

(ii) a supervision order was not
indefinite, but was limited by the requirement that powers be restored when it
appears that the law will be complied with. The Act provided for the immediate

would be conducted by the board according to law;

(iii) any question of whether the
circumstances justified the appointment or continuance of a supervisory
Commission could be determined by a court.

[
119
]

The applicants then argue that, unlike the legislation in
Re
Ottawa Separate Schools
,
Division D does not require unlawful conduct as a
pre-condition for the imposition of supervision, s. 257.31(1) allows the
Minister to request a trusteeship where the Minister has issued a direction
“and in the opinion of the Minister the Board has failed to comply with it”,
Division D does not require the restoration of powers to a separate school
board as soon as it appears it will conduct itself according to law, and that
rather than inviting the scrutiny of a court, Division D precludes it.

[
120
]

In response to the point that the present
Act
does not
provide for the restoration of powers once the schools are conducted according
to law, I do not find the point to have any relevance. In
Re Ottawa Separate
Schools
,
the phrase “according to law” was merely the standard by which the
legislation assessed whether or not a trusteeship should be interposed. Its
only significance was that it was found to be an adequately defined standard.
In this case, the applicable standard is whether or not the board is incurring
a deficit or default, or likely to do so. Similarly, I find this to be an
adequately defined standard. Whether or not a board is in deficit or default,
or likely to be, is a readily assessable standard, a matter of accounting.
Alternatively, the legislation imposes a requirement not to be in deficit; see
s. 231(2). If the board is in deficit it is not being governed “according
to law”. The safeguard of unlawful conduct from
Re Ottawa Separate Schools

is
therefore present.

[
121
]

It is true that the provisions providing for the imposition of a
trusteeship allow a vesting order where the Minister makes a direction
regarding a board’s financial affairs and, in the opinion of the Minister, the
direction is not followed. I agree that this section is, flawed, but not
fatally so. First, the direction must still be with regard to financial
affairs, an important modification. Given that the section is in the
discretion of the Minister, it still provides a rather wide latitude to the
Minister. But, the next consideration is dispositive. As I mentioned above,
although there is discretion there, there is absolutely none as to when the
trusteeship
must
be lifted, i.e. if the financial records disclose that
there is in actuality no deficit.

[
122
]

Finally, as to the preclusion from the scrutiny of a court, I agree
that the protection in
Re Ottawa Separate Schools

was stronger.
Nevertheless, I doubt the effectiveness of the preclusionary clause, s.
257.40(1):

257.40(1)…the Minister has exclusive
jurisdiction as to all matters arising under this Division or out of the
exercise by the board or any person of any of the powers conferred by this
Division, and that jurisdiction is not open to question or review in any
proceeding or by any court.

[
123
]

The invitation to court scrutiny in
Re Ottawa Separate Schools

may
well be preferable to this solicitation. Still, I do not regard that aspect of
Re
Ottawa Separate Schools

as a mandatory factor, in and of itself. In this
case, in the presence of the clear statutory standards, its absence is not
fatal. Furthermore, as I have stated, I would question the ability of the
legislation to preclude
any
court scrutiny. Given that not much time in
argument was spent on this point, and it was not really directly addressed, I
shall refrain from an expansive analysis of the point, and only make a brief
comment.

[
124
]

I do not see this provision as designed to preclude a court
considering whether or not, in a given trusteeship, a s. 93(1) violation
had occurred. Indeed, if such was the intent of the legislation, it would be
invalid. It is not within the constitutional powers and authority of the
legislature to do so. Thus, while the protection of a court is admittedly not
as strong under the present legislation, it is sufficient.

[
125
]

Both applicants and respondents made reference to various provisions
of the
Municipal Affairs Act,
R.S.O. 1990, c. M.46. The respondents submitted
that the trusteeship provisions there demonstrated the powers in the
Education
Act
were not really unusual or untoward. The applicants made the converse
submission, that the powers were far more limited. As I have already decided
that the provisions of the
Education Act
meet the requirements of
Ottawa
Separate School Trustees,
it is unnecessary to consider these other
provisions, and I make no comment in respect thereof.

Disposition

[
126
]

The submissions of the applicants in regard to Division D are rejected.
Because Division D meets the concerns identified in
Ottawa Separate School
Trustees
and
Re Ottawa Separate Schools
,
it is, on its face,
constitutionally valid. There are defined and assessable standards, both for
the imposition and removal of a vesting order. That is all that is necessary to
meet the requirement of s. 93(1).

Issue #3

Do the provisions of Bill 160 contravene

s. 93(1)
of the
Constitution Act, 1867
as it applies to public schools and
the public school system?

Position of the Applicants

[
127
]

The applicants argue that the public school system is
constitutionally protected, and that
Bill 160
contravenes that
protection. In support of this position, the applicants rely on the following
propositions, as stated in their factum:

The case is the first in Ontario to raise
the issue of constitutional protection for the public school system, and
requires that
s. 93
be read and interpreted in this context, rather than,
as in the past, in the context of cases involving the diminution or expansion
of separate school rights;

Mirror equality of the two systems, public
and separate, has existed since before Confederation, and continues to exist.
The two systems have since the
Scott Act
of 1863 exercised the same
rights and powers of local governance, and since then have been treated as
equals by the Legislature up to and including in
Bill 160
; and

Mirror equality or constitutional
reciprocity of the two systems is the only principle which is consistent with
the reasons of the Supreme Court of Canada in
Adler v. Ontario
(1996),

1996 CanLII 148 (SCC)
, 140 D.L.R. (4th) 385 (S.C.C.).

[
128
]

In essence, the public school system claims protection because it
says the rights of a separate school system are illusory without a strong and
independent public system on which to rely for comparison of funding,
governance and choice of attendance.

Position of the Respondents

[
129
]

The respondents reject any suggestion of constitutional protection
for the public school system. They point to the clear wording of
s. 93(1)

which is limited to the rights of any class of persons held at Confederation,
“with respect to Denominational Schools”. The respondents further argue that
Adler
v.
Ontario

(1996),
1996 CanLII 148 (SCC)
, 140 D.L.R. (4th) 385 (S.C.C.), is not authority that

s. 93(1)
confers constitutional status on public schools. They submit that

Adler
is to the contrary. They argue that
Adler
confirms the
province’s plenary power to legislate with regard to public schools and that
public school rights are not themselves constitutionally entrenched.

Analysis

The Majority
Decision in
Adler

[
130
]

In
Adler
,
the Canadian Jewish Congress and the Ontario
Alliance of Christian School Societies asserted a constitutional right to
public funding for private denominational schools. As in the
Reference re
Bill 30,
the applicants’ claims were based on s. 2(
a
) and
s. 15(1) of the
Charter.
They argued in
Adler
,
however, that
their
Charter
rights were violated not only by the public funding
provided exclusively to Roman Catholic schools, but also by the public funding
provided to the public school system to the exclusion of all denominational
schools other than Roman Catholic. Justice Iacobucci summarized his response to
this proposition, at 404 [paras. 40-41]:

The appellants advanced a further argument
which was that, even assuming that Roman Catholic separate schools are given a
privileged place in our constitutional scheme, public schools are given no such
protection. According to this argument, the fact that the government funds
public schools but not private religious schools is analogous to the government
funding, for example, private Christian schools but not private Islamic
schools. As the reasoning goes,
public
schools are not part of the
scheme envisioned by s. 93 and are, thus, open to
Charter
challenge.

In my view, this argument is mistaken in
supposing that public schools are not contemplated by the terms of
s. 93
,
as it applies to Ontario. On
the contrary, the public schools system is an integral part of the s. 93
scheme… A closer examination of s. 93, in particular s. 93(1), as it
applies to the Province of
Ontario, will help to illustrate that the public school system is impliedly,
but nonetheless clearly, contemplated by the terms of that section.

[
131
]

It is this latter part of the majority decision in
Adler
,
dealing
with the argument that public funding to the public school system to the
exclusion of other schools was a
Charter
violation, which the applicants
in this case seek to rely upon.

[
132
]

The applicants submit that two distinct sources of the
constitutional position of public schools are identified in
Adler
.
The
first source the applicants identify is the fact that prior to Confederation,
the rights of the separate system which thereby were entrenched were identified
with reference to, and as a reflection of, the rights and powers of the public
system. The second source is the fact that Roman Catholics had a right to
choose to support either the separate system or the public system. The
following passages from the judgment of Justice Iacobucci, at 406, 407 [paras.
45-47], are relevant to this argument:

This inclusion of public schools in the
Constitution is consistent with the historical purpose of
s. 93
… Thus,
when separate school supporters were negotiating the terms of
s. 93
, they
were negotiating against the back-drop of the existing common school system… As
Wilson J. pointed out in
Reference re Bill 30, supra,
at p. 1193,
at the time
s. 93
was being negotiated, it was assumed the publicly funded
non-denominational schools would always be a part of the political landscape:

“The security afforded the Roman Catholic
minority through the tying of funding for its schools to a proportion of the
funding for the common schools was in the certainty that the Legislature would
never cut off funding for the common schools.”

At the time of Confederation, Roman
Catholic parents could choose to support either the local separate schools or
the local common schools. Section 14 of the
Scott Act
lays out the
registration procedure to be followed. If a parent chose to register as a
separate school supporter, then his or her child would be eligible to attend
only the local separate school.
An Act respecting Common Schools in Upper
Canada,
C.S.U.C. 1859, c. 64, s. 27(16). In other words, Roman
Catholic parents could choose between two publicly funded educational
systems—one Roman Catholic, the other non-denominational.
Section 93
gives
constitutional protection to this publicly funded choice. Therefore, the public
school system is an integral part of the Confederation compromise and,
consequently, receives a protection against constitutional or
Charter
attack.

This protection exists despite the fact
that public school rights are not themselves constitutionally entrenched. It is
the province’s plenary power to legislate with regard to public schools, which
are open to all members of society, without distinction, that is
constitutionally entrenched. This is what creates the immunity from
Charter
scrutiny.
To paraphrase Wilson L, in
Reference re Bill 30, supra,
at p. 1198,
funding for public schools is insulated from
Charter
attack as legislation
enacted pursuant to the plenary education power granted to the provincial
legislatures as part of the Confederation compromise. If the plenary power is
so insulated, then so is the proper exercise of it.

[
133
]

The applicants assert that, if the public school system is
“impliedly” contemplated by the terms of s. 93(1), then there are limits
on the provincial power to legislate with respect to the public system. The
applicants further submit in their factum:

The “publicly funded choice” which Roman
Catholics have as a constitutional right gives implicit constitutional
protection to the public system. As that constitutional choice is the right of
Roman Catholics to have their children educated in either the separate system
or the public system, it must follow that the public system must also be
constitutionally protected. It is not only a public system which is protected
but the elements of
the
public system which existed in 1867.

For the choice to have substance and
reality, it must be a choice between two equal systems, each having the twin
attributes of the pre-Confederation structure, equal rights to Provincial
funding and equal powers of access to their respective local resources.
Clearly, the sponsors of the
Scott Act
intended that Roman Catholics
have access to a system of their own, equal in status to the public system.
Otherwise the “choice” is illusory.

[
134
]

Justice Campbell, in the
Ontario
Public School
Boards Assn. v.
Ontario
(Attorney General)
(1997),
1997 CanLII 12352 (ON CTGD)
, 151 D.L.R. (4th) 346 (Ont. Ct. (Gen. Div.)) (“
Fewer
School Boards
”),

rejected this argument, at 366, 367:

The court in
Adler

held that

s. 93
gave the public school system a measure of protection. But the
protection in
Adler

was not denominational protection.
Adler
protects
the public school system only against
Charter
challenges of the kind
asserted in that case … That case holds only that the public school system,
because it is an integral part of the overall s. 93 scheme, is therefore
immune from
Charter
attack because one part of the constitution cannot be
used to attack another part of the constitution.

…

Adler
is a
shield to protect the public school system against
Charter
challenges.
Adler

is not a sword to win denominational rights for public schools.

[
135
]

I am in full agreement with Justice Campbell. When the majority in
Adler

states that the public school system is “an integral part” of the

s. 93
scheme, it means that the existence of a publicly funded public
school cannot give rise to a
Charter
infringement vis-à-vis religious
private schools. Similarly, the existence of a publicly funded Roman Catholic
separate system cannot give rise to a
Charter
infringement vis-à-vis the
schools of other religions. Given, however, the rather extensive and well
argued submissions of the applicants on the mirror image issue, it is
appropriate to review them further.

[
136
]

At the outset, I would observe that I take issue with the
applicants’ characterization of
Adler
as providing two distinct sources
of a constitutional position of the public school system. Justice Iacobucci’s words
certainly are capable of this construction but, given the context within his
reasons, I do not find that the reference to a “choice” provides a separate
source for the alleged constitutional position of public schools. Much of the
relevant discussion is taken up with an explanation of the fact that separate
school supporters sought to tie their rights to those of the public school
system, as that system could set a standard against which separate school
supporters could measure their rights. In my opinion, Justice Iacobucci’s
reasons are focused on the concept of the public school system as a
“back-drop”. It is my view that his reference to the ability of separate school
supporters to choose between the respective systems is no more than an
elaboration of the point, that the separate school supporters were bargaining
in the shadow of the public school system.

[
137
]

What then of this “choice” or “back-drop”? Does it provide the
mirror image rights that the applicants seek? Do the applicants have similar
rights and privileges to those of separate school supporters, because of this
“choice” or “backdrop”? In my estimation, if this “choice” or “backdrop” has
any real significance, it is only as a reference point, and nothing more.

[
138
]

With respect, in my view, the flaw in the applicants’ argument
becomes apparent when one considers the words they have used to support it,
“constitutional reciprocity”. The choice of the word “reciprocity” illustrates
the reasoning the applicants rely on: the separate school system uses the
public school system as a frame of reference, to determine if it is receiving
appropriate treatment by the majority, as expressed by the will of the
legislature. Therefore, this reasoning goes, the public school system is
entitled to use the separate school system as a term of reference, to determine
if it is receiving appropriate treatment from the majority, as expressed by the
will of the legislature. Put even more crudely, the reciprocity argument says
that because what we get you get, what you get we get. I mean no disrespect to
the very able arguments of counsel when I phrase things in this fashion. It is
simply that by framing the argument in these terms, it demonstrates how the
applicants are relying on a false syllogism.

[
139
]

To explicate further: a syllogism may be described as a form of
reasoning in which from two propositions a third is deduced. Where the
deduction is unwarranted or invalid, the syllogism is a false one. A simple
example of a false syllogism is (1) apples are fruit (2) oranges are fruit (3)
therefore oranges are apples. In this case, the first premise of the applicants
is that the separate school system has constitutional recognition. The second
premise is that the public school system has constitutional recognition (as I
discuss below, one possible interpretation of
Adler

is that the public
school system has some recognition, to the extent that there may be a right to
some public funding. It is not, for the purposes of this argument, necessary to
decide whether or not
Adler
actually stands for that proposition.
Therefore, solely for the purpose of present analysis, I assume without
deciding that
Adler
constitutionally protects
a
right of public
funding for a public school system.) The deduction which follows, in the
applicants’ argument, from these two premises, is that because both school
systems have a constitutional existence, they both have exactly the same
constitutional rights. In my view, this is an invalid deduction, and therefore
the syllogism is a false one.

[
140
]

Just because the public school system is impliedly contemplated by

s. 93(1)
, it does not follow that the public school system is entitled to
the same rights and privileges as the denominational schools under

s. 93(1)
. It is necessary to ask
why
the public school system is impliedly
contemplated by
s. 93(1)
.

[
141
]

Consider the ultimate purpose of
s. 93(1)
: the maintenance and
preservation of a separate school system, and its Catholicity. Can the
preservation of a public system also be said to be an ultimate goal of

s. 93(1)
? The applicants reject Justice Campbell’s observation that the
mirror equality argument seeks to win denominational rights for the public
schools. Perhaps they are correct. But there’s the rub. If the applicants’
are
not
seeking denominational rights, then they cannot be said to be within
the contemplation of the ultimate goal of
s. 93(1)
, being the preservation
of a denominational school system, infused with Catholicism.

[
142
]

If the applicants do not share the goal of
s. 93(1)
, then the
argument for full reciprocity falls away. The two systems are not to be treated
equally because they each represent independent purposes of
s. 93(1)
.
Rather, insofar as
s. 93(1)
contemplates the public school system, it is
contemplated only as a reference point or a means to an end.

[
143
]

This conclusion is also evident from the decisions of other courts.
In
Re Calgary Board of Education and Attorney-General for Alberta
(1979),

1979 CanLII 1187 (AB QB)
, 106 D.L.R. (3d) 415 (Alta. Q.B.), Stevenson J. was dealing with a challenge by
the public board to legislation granting new corporate tax rights to separate
school boards. The question was whether the Alberta equivalent of
s. 93(1)
, s. 17(1), could protect public
schools. Justice Stevenson rebuffed this proposition, at 421:

I come to the conclusion that s-s. (1)
is protective legislation. It guarantees certain rights to the minority
residents and the boards established by them and it does not lie in the mouth
of the public board to attack legislation on the basis that its rights are
prejudiced.

[
144
]

The applicants seek to distinguish this case on two bases. First,
that the Alberta situation
differs, in that Roman Catholics do not have a choice about supporting separate
school boards. Second, that the case was dealing with an expansion of separate
school rights, not a contraction of public school ones. With regard to the
first distinction, I make no assessment of its accuracy; Re Schmidt and Calgary
Board of Education (1976),
1976 ALTASCAD 157 (CanLII)
, 72 D.L.R. (3d) 330 (Alta. S.C.A.D.), may or may not
stand for this proposition. It is irrelevant for present purposes because, as I
have said, in Adler, Justice Iacobucci’s real concern was in respect of the
concept of the public school system as a backdrop. With regard to the second
distinction, I agree that it is a valid point, but I think it is obviated by
the more sweeping remarks of the Court of Appeal in its affirmation of Justice
Stevenson’s decision, in Re Calgary Board of Education and Attorney-General for
Alberta (1981),
1981 ABCA 29 (CanLII)
, 122 D.L.R. (3d) 249 (C.A.). McDermid J.A., speaking for a five
member panel, commented that for all practical purposes s. 17 of the Alberta constitutional legislation, and s,
93(1), were identical. At 251, McDermid J.A. stated:

The relevant wording… is exactly the same
as to protection of the minority. The intention was to protect the minority
leaving the majority to protect themselves through the use of the democratic
instrument, the ballot box.

[
145
]

This wording was picked up on, and reiterated, by the entire panel
of the Alberta Court of Appeal in
Alberta
Public School Boards’ Assn. v.
Alberta
(Attorney General)
in its rejection of
the mirror image argument in that case.

[
146
]

Justice McDermid’s passage demonstrates once again that while the
public school system may or may not have a role to play under
s. 93(1)
,
its role is limited to supporting the separate school system. Protection of the
public school system is not an independent goal.

[
147
]

I hasten to add that this is not a qualitative judgment about
separate and public schools. I realize the effect of a discussion which appears
to raise separate school rights above those of public schools, and treat the
existence of a public system as merely supportive of the continued viability of
the separate system, may also appear to some to suggest a value judgment about
the respective worth of the two systems. That is neither the intent nor the
point of the foregoing discussion. The constitutional existence of separate
schools versus the constitutional non-existence of public schools is merely a
recognition that constitutional protection of one system was deemed necessary
while constitutional protection of the other was not.

[
148
]

This, in turn, is a reflection of the nature of constitutional
instruments. They often serve to protect individuals from the state, or to
demarcate functions of various parts of the state. Federalism sets out the
boundaries between the provinces and the federal government. The
Canadian
Charter of Rights and Freedoms

to some extent at least, seeks to protect
the individual from the power of the state. Section 93(1) also serves as a
historical form of minority protection. The public school system can make no
such claim. It did not require a constitutional goal independent from that of
the separate school system, because, as Justice McDermid so appropriately puts
it, the majority could protect itself through the democratic instrument. While
the present case demonstrates that there can be rather strong disagreements
among the body politic, the implication of the applicants’ argument is that the
majority needs protection from the majority.

[
149
]

This analysis does not completely dispose of the argument of the
applicants. But, it does cast doubt on the syllogism which lies at the heart of
their argument. True reciprocity would require the two systems to have
identical status under
s. 93(1)
. Perhaps—without, to emphasize once more,
deciding the point—
Adler

provides the public school system with a
measure of protection. The protection, such as it is, is only that protection
necessary to preserve denominational schools. In my view, this is the
interpretation which is most consistent with
Adler
,
and follows from
Justice Iacobucci’s reasons at 406, 407, set out above.

[
150
]

Accordingly, I reject the applicants’ submission that “it is not
only
a
public system which is protected but the elements of
the
public
system which existed in 1867”.

[
151
]

The applicants are still left with the argument that the public
system is a necessary reference point. Taken at its highest, one might assert
that
Adler
stands for the proposition that there has to be
a
publicly
funded system. Assume for the sake of argument that this proposition is true.
It does not provide the applicants with any solace. The continued existence and
funding of a public system through
Bill 160
is not in dispute.
Accordingly, an absolute level of funds will be provided to the public system,
and the separate system will be able to look at its funding, to determine
whether it is receiving an equivalent amount. Thus, there is a framework for
the separate system to evaluate itself against, which is all that is necessary.

[
152
]

While the separate system funding level may be a reflection of the
public system funding level, the rights and privileges of the public system are
not a reflection of the rights and privileges of the separate system. Consider
the argument offered by OECTA, that
Bill 160
prejudicially interferes
with its rights of management and control Assume for the moment that this
argument is correct. It is still necessary to acknowledge that separate school
supporters have some right of management and control in order to preserve the
separate nature of their system. The goal is separateness or Catholicity. Some
argument was made that an “aspects” analysis had no application in Ontario, and that a complete system, with
the attendant complete rights was necessary for separate school supporters. The
suggestion then followed that if the denominational school supporters required
a distinct system with reserved powers to preserve the goal of Catholicity,
then the public school system must also be distinct, and have the same reserved
powers.

[
153
]

In my opinion, this argument serves as a further illustration as to
why the syllogism on which the applicants rely is invalid. Neither “aspects”
nor a distinct system with reserved powers are constitutional goals. They are
means to the end of preserving Catholicity, albeit some powers may be so
closely entwined with the achievement of the goal that they are entrenched
themselves. Some powers, be they “aspects” or a complete system, may be
necessary to the separate system in order to preserve its separate nature,
achieving the goal of preserving Catholicity. In contrast, the public system
needs no such constitutional powers, as it has no constitutional goal. It is a
constitutional means. As long as the public system exists, it preserves the
choice of separate supporters.

The Minority
Decision in
Adler

[
154
]

The applicants also point to the reasons of Mr. Justice
Sopinka, Major J. concurring, in an attempt to surmount what I have described
as the limited constitutional nature of the public school system. The
applicants rely on Sopinka J.’s reasons as “the minority’s interpretation of
the majority reasons”. Counsel suggested that it was not necessary to speculate
on the effect of
Adler,
because Sopinka J. tells us what the effect is.

[
155
]

Justice Sopinka disagreed with the proposition that
s. 93(1)

extended any protection to the public schools from
Charter

attack. At
435 [paras. 141-2], he comments:

The second proposition advanced by my
colleague which serves to insulate the impugned legislation from
Charter

scrutiny
under
s. 15
is that pre-Confederation legislation equated certain rights
and privileges of separate schools to those of public schools and thereby
impliedly brought these rights and privileges within the protection of
s. 93(1). Not all rights and privileges of public schools existing at
Confederation are protected, just those that relate to the existence of public
schools “which are open to all members of society, without distinction”.

I note at the outset that this proposition
erroneously assumes that because certain rights and privileges of the
Protestant majoritarian schools are relevant in identifying the rights and
privileges of separate schools, the former are
ipso facto
given
constitutional protection. My colleague says that “public schools are part and
parcel of
s. 93
’s comprehensive Code”. But, the rights and privileges of
public schools are merely the benchmarks for ascertaining the rights and
privileges of separate schools. Certain provisions of pre-Confederation
statutes gave separate schools the same rights as enjoyed by public schools.
While the terms of those statutes are relevant to ascertain what these rights
and privileges were, the statutes themselves are not given constitutional
status. Only the rights and privileges of separate schools were given
constitutional protection.

[
156
]

Justice Sopinka clearly differed from the majority on the full
implication of using the public school system as a frame of reference, or, to
use his word, benchmark, In his view, while the public school system was useful
as a benchmark, it received no protection as such. Sopinka J.’s analysis, while
rejecting entrenchment of a public right to funding, clearly recognized the
utility of the public school system to the separate system as a frame of
reference. Because both sets of reasons recognize the value of the public
school system as a standard of reference, I think that it is fair to say the
two judgments walk down the same road a fair distance together.

[
157
]

Where the two sets of reasons may part company is on the proposition
that
s. 93(1)
entrenches at least
a
public system. I am not really
sure that the majority reasons do stand for this proposition, and, as I have
suggested above, it is not necessary to decide that point in this case. But, it
is certainly a fair reading of Justice Sopinka’s judgment to say that he saw
the majority judgment as entrenching a public right to funding. Justice Sopinka
objected to the proposition that funding might be protected, on the grounds
that there was no logical distinction between a funding right and any other
right. At 431 [para. 125] he summarized his objection to any constitutional
status:

If s. 93 protects the rights and
privileges of the public schools, then all rights and privileges at
Confederation must be included. There is no basis for concluding that while all
rights and privileges of denominational schools are protected, the only
privilege protected relating to public schools is funding.

[
158
]

I do not take this passage to mean that Justice Sopinka thinks the
majority has entrenched a wide series of rights and privileges relating to
public schools. To my mind, the passage has two possible meanings. First, that
it is illogical to entrench funding without other rights, and that therefore
neither should be entrenched. On this reading, Justice Sopinka clearly does not
suggest the majority have entrenched rights and privileges. Rather, he is
suggesting that one right, funding, has been entrenched by the majority
decision, where none should have been.

[
159
]

The second meaning the passage could have, is that Justice Sopinka
is warning of the ramifications of entrenching funding, cautioning that such
entrenchment could have further implications. While this is more nuanced than
the first interpretation, in that it suggests the possible entrenchment of
rights and privileges, one must be clear that Justice Sopinka is warning
against such an extension. He is not saying that it has been done.

[
160
]

So, on one approach to Justice Sopinka’s reasons, he is not even
suggesting that rights and privileges of the public school system have been
entrenched. On the other approach, he is only cautioning against what he sees
as unfortunate implications.

[
161
]

The applicants’ submission that the Court should be guided by
Sopinka J.’s analysis of the majority overlooks the first possible
interpretation of his reasons. Moreover, the applicants’ submission in this
regard misses the fact that Justice Sopinka was only discussing implications
and ramifications; the effect of the applicants’ submission is to turn Justice
Sopinka’s
warning
into a self-fulfilling prophecy. Indeed, perhaps the
best use of the minority decision is to treat it as an added reason to approach
with caution the application of the majority reasons.

[
162
]

Consequently, although I appreciate that Justice Sopinka’s reasons provide
a useful contrast to and illustration of the majority decision, I cannot agree
that his reasons require me to treat public school rights and privileges as
being entrenched.

Disposition

[
163
]

The applicants’ submissions on the mirror image issue are rejected.
The public school system cannot find any entrenched rights and privileges in
s. 93(1), except perhaps a right of existence, which is not necessary for
me to decide on the facts of this case.

Issue #4

If the provisions of Bill 160 do not
contravene
s. 93(1)
of the
Constitution Act, 1867
, do the provisions of
Bill 160 which take away the power of school boards to determine and levy
property tax rates for school purposes nonetheless contravene constitutional
convention?

[
164
]

OECTA took no position on this issue. As well, given my disposition
in respect of issue #1, this issue has relevance only in respect of public
school boards. However, it is nevertheless addressed as a general issue.

Position of the Applicants

[
165
]

The applicants submit that the unprotected party or parties still
find protection by way of reliance on the concept of a constitutional
convention. The applicants submit that such a convention arises in regard to
the right of boards to levy and determine property taxes because such a right
was a fundamental term of Confederation and, therefore, cannot be unilaterally
altered by the provincial government.

Position of the Respondents

[
166
]

The respondents submit that even where constitutional conventions
exist they are not capable of enforcement by a court and, furthermore, that in
all events no such convention exists.

Analysis

[
167
]

The applicants’ submissions must be rejected. The first and last
reason for rejecting the applicants’ submissions is that regardless of whether
or not there is in fact any such constitutional convention as the one
submitted, it cannot be applied so as to strike down or overrule a clear and
specific law. There is clear authority from the Supreme Court to this effect;
whatever their other uses may be, constitutional conventions cannot be used to
invalidate express and definite legal rules. In
Reference re: Amendment of
the Constitution of
Canada

(1981),
1981 CanLII 25 (SCC)
, 125 D.L.R. (3d) 1 (S.C.C.), the
Court explained the purpose of constitutional conventions, at 84:

The main purpose of constitutional
conventions is to ensure that the legal framework of the Constitution will be
operated in accordance with the prevailing constitutional values or principles
of the period. For example, the constitutional value which is the pivot of the
conventions stated above and relating to responsible government is the
democratic principle: the powers of the State must be exercised in accordance
with the wishes of the electorate…

[
168
]

The Court went on to state, in a resounding and unambiguous
ratio,

that conventions could not be enforced by the courts, at 84, 85:

The conventional rules of the Constitution
present one striking peculiarity. In contradistinction to the laws of the
Constitution, they are not enforced by the Courts. One reason for this
situation is that, unlike common law miles, conventions are not judge made
rules. They are not based on judicial precedents but on precedents established
by the institutions of government themselves. Nor are they in the nature of
statutory commands which it is the function and duty of the Courts to obey and
enforce. Furthermore, to enforce them would mean to administer some formal
sanction when they are breached. But the legal system from which they are
distinct does not contemplate formal sanctions for their breach.

Perhaps the main reason why conventional
rules cannot be enforced by the Courts is that they are generally in conflict
with the legal rules which they postulate and the Courts are bound to enforce
the legal rules.
The conflict is not of a type
which would entail the commission of any illegality. It results from the fact
that legal rules create wide powers, discretions and rights which conventions
prescribe should be exercised only in a certain limited manner, if at all.
[Emphasis added.]

[
169
]

The minority, who dissented as to the actual existence of a
constitutional convention in that case, were, however, equally unambiguous as
to the effect of its existence, at 111:

As has been pointed out by the majority, a
fundamental difference between the legal, that is the statutory and common law
rules of the Constitution, and the conventional rules is that, while a breach
of the legal rules, whether of statutory or common law nature, has a legal
consequence in that it will be restrained by the Courts, no such sanction
exists for breach or non-observance of the conventional rules. The observance
of constitutional conventions depends upon the acceptance of the obligation of
conformance by the actors deemed to be bound thereby. When this consideration
is insufficient to compel observance no Court may enforce the convention by
legal action. The sanction for non-observance of a convention is political in
that disregard of a convention may lead to political defeat, to loss of office,
or to other political consequences, but it will not engage the attention of the
Courts which are limited to matters of law alone. Courts, however, may
recognize the existence of conventions and that is what is asked of us in
answering the questions. The answer, whether affirmative or negative, however,
can have no legal effect, and acts performed or done in conformance with the
law, even though in direct contradiction of well-established conventions, will
not be enjoined or set aside by the Courts.

[
170
]

In order to surmount these rather convincing holdings, the
applicants make the following propositions. This decision was made before the
patriation of the Constitution in 1982.
Section 52
of the
Constitution Act,
1982
,
being Schedule B to the
Canada
Act, 1982
(U.K.), 1982, c. 11, enacted as part of the patriation package, requires
that any laws inconsistent with the provisions of the Constitution be held to
be of no force and effect, to the extent of the inconsistency. The Supreme
Court has held that s. 52(2), defining the instruments of the
Constitution, is not limited to the documents in that section. Therefore, the
argument goes, the Constitution that s. 52(1) is applicable to, includes
constitutional conventions. Accordingly, the applicants submit that, “a court
when faced with a law which is inconsistent with a constitutional convention
has an obligation to declare that law, to the extent necessary, of no force and
effect”.

[
171
]

The respondents answer that the proposition that constitutional
conventions are not enforced by courts is not changed by
s. 52(1)
of the
Constitution
Act, 1982
.
The Constitution has always been the “supreme law of Canada” and the courts have always had the
authority to declare invalid any law inconsistent with the constitution.

[
172
]

I agree. As a basic proposition, it is clear that where an action
violated the terms of a recognized constitutional document in a justiciable
way, the courts would freely declare it
ultra vires.
The point really
is, as
Reference re Amendment of the Constitution
notes, that
conventions, while they may be “part” of the constitution, are not a justiciable
part.

[
173
]

What is more, the applicants’ argument fails to recognize the
perhaps subtle distinction between a freestanding constitutional convention
which is not truly justiciable, and the recognition of a power or powers that
have always been implicit in a constitutional document (but were hitherto
unexplored), and are justiciable. Consider the case the applicants cite in
support of their proposition that the Constitution applies to unwritten
documents,
New Brunswick Broadcasting Co. v. Nova Scotia
(
Speaker,
House of Assembly
) (1993),
1993 CanLII 153 (SCC)
, 100 D.L.R. (4th) 212 (S.C.C.).

[
174
]

In this case, the Court was concerned with the power of the Nova
Scotia Speaker of the Assembly to exclude television cameras from the
legislature. The argument was made that this action violated
Charter

guarantees.
Madam Justice McLachlin rejected the argument on the basis that there was an
unwritten law that the inherent privileges of the legislature encompassed a
right to exclude strangers. In that case an unwritten law was being used to protect
one part of the Constitution from another. That is a far cry from the present
situation where a putative convention is being asserted to invalidate state
action. More importantly though, I do not read Madam Justice McLachlin’s
decision as supporting an application of constitutional conventions. At 264,
265, she states:

It seems indisputable that the inherent
privileges of Canada’s
legislative bodies, those “certain very moderate privileges which were
necessary for the maintenance of order and discipline during the performance of
their duties”… fall within the group of principles constitutionalized by virtue
of this preamble. The principles constitutionalized in this manner were seen to
be unwritten and unexpressed; I do not understand the entrenchment of written
rights guarantees, or the adoption of specific written instruments, to negate
the manifest intention expressed in the preamble of our Constitution that Canada retain the fundamental
constitutional tenets upon which British parliamentary democracy rested. This
is not a case of importing an unexpressed concept into our constitutional
regime, but of recognizing a legal power fundamental to the constitutional
regime which Canada had adopted
in its
Constitution Acts, 1867 to 1982. Nor are we here treating a mere
convention to which the courts have not given legal effect; the authorities
indicate that the legal status of inherent privileges has never been in doubt.
[Emphasis
added.]

[
175
]

The emphasized passage does not appear to support the applicants’
position. More importantly, I see this passage as demonstrating a distinction
between conventions and implicit powers.
New Brunswick Broadcasting
addresses
the fact that legislative bodies are explicit constitutional entities, and in
order to perform their constitutionally appointed roles, there are certain
rights and privileges which must accrue to them.

[
176
]

I see this analysis as analogous to the sort of analysis that courts
have long performed in regard to
s. 96
of the
Constitution Act, 1867
.
The

s. 96
analysis determined that the provision for a federal appointing
power meant that the institution of an independent judiciary, and the core
jurisdiction necessary to it, were implicit in the Constitution; see for
instance
MacMillan Bloedel Ltd. v. Simpson
(1995),
1995 CanLII 57 (SCC)
, 130 D.L.R. (4th) 385
(S.C.C.). In the same way,
New Brunswick Broadcasting
merely determined
that certain powers were inherent to and implicit in the existence of
legislatures.

[
177
]

In fact, a similar example can be drawn from the present case. Had
the applicants’ “mirror equality” argument (discussed above under issue #3)
succeeded, it would have been a recognition of a right implicit in s. 93.
After all, nowhere in the text of s. 93 is there a suggestion of
constitutional status for public school boards. So, if the applicants had been
correct, the Court would have been interpreting the Constitution to find an
unwritten, but necessary right or power. The fact that the applicants were
unsuccessful on their “mirror equality” in s. 93 argument reinforces the point
that they cannot succeed on the constitutional convention submission.

[
178
]

To be sure, it is not that constitutional conventions have no legal
application whatsoever; at the very least they are undoubtedly useful as an
interpretative aid. This application appears to be consistent with the
observations of Madam Justice Russell in
Alberta
Public School
Boards’ Assn. v.
Alberta
(Attorney General),
at paragraphs 43 and 47:

Within the limits of its fundamental
nature, the Constitution is adaptable and does not articulate the full extent
of its operating principles. The full scope of its legal norms is to be found
in the vast array of judicial interpretations of its explicit provisions
through a variety of interpretive aids.

…

While we endorse the concept of implicit
constitutional norms, those norms must be grounded in the natural limits of the
language of the Constitution, and accepted constitutional principles respecting
the scheme of federalism. In our view, neither that language, nor any
constitutional principle supports the notion of an entrenched reasonable
autonomy for school boards, with the exception of the express and limited
protection given to separate schools by virtue of
s. 93
of the
Constitution
Act, 1867
,
and various provincial constitutions.

[
179
]

By way of example, it might be said that a proscription against
warrantless home searches has long been part of the law of our country. But,
prior to the enshrinement of the prohibition against unreasonable search and
seizure in the
Charter
,
the federal government might legitimately have
passed a law violating this prohibition, and as long as the language was
sufficiently clear, the law would have been enforceable. A court might have
construed the statute strictly, but if it was clear enough, it could do
nothing. The same is true of constitutional conventions.

[
180
]

The foregoing essentially disposes of the constitutional convention
argument. There is, however, one more point to mention in passing. Whatever the
application of conventions, it seems extremely unlikely that any such putative
convention as the one proposed by the applicants could exist. For such a
convention to exist, it would be an expansion of an explicitly defined right in

s. 93
, in the face of another explicitly defined capacity, the province’s
power to legislate in this field. And note that the province’s power is not
just any power; it is power which is
plenary
within its field. In
respect of this point, I cannot improve on the words of Mr. Justice
Campbell in the
Fewer School Boards
case, at 362:

…the constitution must be understood,
subject to changing times, to provide the core content of the things it
actually deals with such as denominational school rights.

The content of constitutionally vested
denominational rights has to be interpreted by the courts from time to time in
light of changing social conditions. But it is still the constitutional rights
expressly secured by the original constitutional pact that are being
interpreted, not some penumbral shadow of extra-constitutional convention
unsecured by that constitutional pact. In respect of matters such as
denominational school rights explicitly covered by the constitution, it is
difficult to think that the constitution does not mean exactly what it says, no
more and no less, as interpreted by the courts from time to time in light of
changing circumstances and the need to preserve access of educational
opportunity.

[
181
]

This reasoning is also inherent, in my view, in the decision of
Madam Justice Russell, in
Alberta
Public School Boards’ Assn. v.
Alberta
(Attorney General).

Disposition

[
182
]

The submission of the applicants, that they can rely on a
constitutional convention in order to retain the right to levy and determine taxes,
is rejected. It is very doubtful that any such convention exists and, if it
did, it would not be enforceable.

Issue
#5

Are the provisions of Bill 160, which confer
on the executive branch of government legislative powers with respect to
education, unconstitutional in that they violate and undermine the
“
rule of law
”
and the principle of effective
representation through responsible taxation?

In brief, does the extent to which
Bill 160
provides
for delegation undermine the rule of law?

Position of the Applicants

[
183
]

The applicants submit that in its cumulative effect,
Bill 160
is
inconsistent with the system of government contemplated by the
Constitution
Act, 1867
.
They submit that the breadth and significance of the matters
consigned to regulatory control, in concert with the absence of any justiciable
standards or limits applicable to those powers are inconsistent with
fundamental constitutional principles.

Position of the Respondents

[
184
]

The respondents submit that
Bill 160
does not provide for
unrestricted delegation, and such delegation as is granted in
Bill 160
is
within the jurisdiction of the provincial legislature and is consistent with
the principle of the rule of law.

Analysis

[
185
]

At its core, the submission of the applicants is that the government
has gone too far and delegated too much, with respect to the taxing power and
other regulatory powers in the educational system. Aside from the power of the
Minister of Finance to set tax rates contained in s. 257.12 of the
Education
Act,
the applicants refer to the following set of regulatory powers:

s. 1(6) Permanent Improvements

s. 43.1 Supporter Non-Resident
Attendance Rights;

s. 43.2 Non-Supporter Resident
Attendance Rights Based on Business Property;

s. 46.1(4) Residence on Defence
Property

s. 56 Territory without Municipal
Organization in Area of Jurisdiction of a School Authority;

s. 86.1 Extension of Boundaries

[Page 324]

s. 135(32) Exceptions Regarding Successor
Board Determinations;

s. 170(3) School Councils;

s. 170.1(5) Class Size;

s. 170.3 Teacher Assistants;

s. 191.1(3) School Authority Honorariums;

s. 195(7) Land Reserved as a School Site;

s. 208.1 Electronic Meetings;

s. 257.12 Tax Rates;

s. 257.14(1) and s. 257.27 Tax
Notices;

s. 257.19 Tax Collection;

s. 266.5(1) Educational Institutions and
Training Institutions; and

s. 287.1(2) Terms and Conditions of
Employment for Principals and Vice Principals.

[
186
]

The applicants assert that while the power of the Legislature to
enact laws in relation to education implies a power to act through the
Executive by conferring reasonable regulation-making powers there must be some
limitation on this ability. The applicants assert that the power of delegation
through
Bill 160
is completely unfettered and that this is contrary to
both the rule of law and also to the principle of effective representation
through responsible government. This submission is based upon a combination of
the concepts of delegation and vagueness.

Delegation

[
187
]

With regard to the power of delegation, the only constitutional
requirement is, as the
Fewer School Boards
case notes, that the powers
of delegation be explicitly set out in the statute. This has long been the case
in Canada.

[
188
]

Neil Finkelstein in
Laskin’s Canadian Constitutional Law,
5th
ed. (Toronto: Carswell, 1986), summarizes the constitutional permissibility of
legislative delegation in the following manner, at 42:

There is nothing express in the
Constitution
Act
about delegation, but ever since
Hodge v. The Queen
(1883), 9
App Cas. 117 (P.C.)
it has been clear that the maxim
delegatus non
potest delegare
has no constitutional significance relative to the
delegation of legislative power by Parliament or provincial legislature to some
other subordinate agency:

[
189
]

Hodge v. The Queen
(1883), 9 App.
Cas. 117 (P.C.)
, is the foundation case for a wide power of delegation. In
that case the Privy Council was confronted with the argument that provincial
legislatures, as delegates of the federal Parliament, had no power to
subdelegate. The Privy Council rejected this contention, holding that the
provinces were as sovereign in their assigned constitutional areas as
Parliament was in its, and that the provinces had a wide power of delegation.

[
190
]

Building on
Hodge
are the two major
War Measures Act
cases;

Re Gray
(1918),
1918 CanLII 533 (SCC)
, 42 D.L.R. 1 (S.C.C.), and
Reference re Regulations
(Chemicals) Under War Measures Act,
1943 CanLII 1 (SCC)
, [1943] 1 D.L.R. 248 (S.C.C.). Both
cases dealt with regulations enacted under the extremely vague and wide power
bestowed upon the government by s. 3 of the
War Measures Act
[see
War
Measures Act,
R.S.C. 1927, c. 206]:

3(1) The Governor in Council may do and
authorize such acts and things, and to make from time to time such orders and
regulations, as he may by reason of the existence of real or apprehended war,
invasion or insurrection, deem necessary or advisable for the security,
defence, peace, order and welfare of Canada…

[
191
]

Some flavour for the wide delegation that the Court deemed
constitutional can be found in Fitzpatrick J.’s judgment in
Gray,
at
2-3:

The practice of authorizing administrative
bodies to make regulations to carry out the object of an Act, instead of
setting out all the details in the Act itself, is well known and its legality
unquestioned

…

Parliament cannot, indeed, abdicate its
functions, but within reasonable limits at any rate it can delegate its powers
to the executive government. Such powers must necessarily be subject to
determination at any time by Parliament and needless to say the acts of the
executive, under its delegated authority, must fall within the ambit of the
legislative pronouncement by which its authority is measured.

[
192
]

Chemicals
also clearly sets out the
ability of a legislature to delegate extremely widely. Professor Bora Laskin
commented on
Chemicals
in “Administrative Law—War—Subdelegation of
Legislative Power Without Express Statutory Authorization” (1943), 21 Can. Bar Rev. 141. Professor Laskin (later
Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of Canada) observed that the American
doctrine of delegation, born out of a more rigorous conception of separation of
powers, had little application to this country. At 145 he notes:

Certainly there is no constitutional
problem which surrounds delegation in Canada as it does in the United States.

[
193
]

And, at 147:

Even in the field of agency, in which it
has its primary application, the maxim [
delegatus non potest delegare
]
is not literally true. That it has been invoked in American constitutional law
has been due not so much to its intrinsic force as to reliance on the terms of
the national and state constitutions and on the political doctrine of
separation of powers.

[
194
]

The strength of
Hodge, Gray,
and
Chemicals
was
confirmed in
Attorney General of Nova Scotia v. Attorney General of Canada,
1950 CanLII 26 (SCC)
, [1950]
4 D.L.R. 369 (S.C.C.). That case dealt with the ability of the respective
legislative bodies to provide for federal-provincial inter-delegation to
subordinate bodies. The Court referred to the
Hodge
line of delegation,
noting that it was uncontroversial, but of a different nature from what was
before it.

[
195
]

In this case, the requirement of explicit definition has been met.
Consider the very regulation making powers that the applicants have attacked.
The headings provided by the applicants in respect of each regulation making
power (such as “Non-Supporter Resident Attendance Rights”, “Territory without
Municipal Organization in Area of Jurisdiction of a School Authority”, etc.)
appear to be derived from the headings and marginal notes in the
Act,
and
also appear to be a fair representation of the content of each section. The
specificity of these headings suggests little doubt as to what the
Lieutenant-Governor in Council is making regulations in regard to. The
Act
does
not simply say the Lieutenant-Governor in Council may make regulations, full
stop. The
Act
says the Lieutenant-Governor in Council may make
regulations in regard to “Non-Supporter Resident Attendance Rights”, and so on.

Vagueness

[
196
]

On the related point of vagueness, the applicants make reference to
the test found in
R. v.
Nova Scotia
Pharmaceutical Society (No. 2)
(1992),
1992 CanLII 72 (SCC)
, 139
N.R. 241 at 277, 278, 93 D.L.R. (4th) 36 (S.C.C.):

A vague provision does not provide an
adequate basis for legal debate, that is for reaching a conclusion as to its
meaning by reasoned analysis applying legal criteria. It does not sufficiently
delineate any area of risk, and thus can provide neither fair notice to the
citizen nor a limitation of enforcement discretion.

[
197
]

By way of an example of vagueness, the applicants point to the
provision in s. 257.12(1)(
b
), allowing the Minister of Finance to “prescribe
the tax rates for school purposes, for the purpose of section 257,.7”.
Section 257.7 in turn sets out the various bodies, such as municipalities,
which are to collect the taxes according to the designated rates.

[
198
]

With respect, I do not see how this fails to provide “an adequate
basis for legal debate.” The object of the taxes is identified, school
purposes, as is the body or bodies tasked with their collection. Given its
context within the
Education Act,
the meaning of school purposes is also
readily ascertainable; being expenditures connected with schooling, such as the
trustee honoraria provided for in s. 191.

[
199
]

While one can appreciate the applicants’ references to the rule of
law, and to the possibility that the regulation-making powers entrusted to the
government by
Bill 160
are indeed very extensive, the statutory
provisions fulfill the necessary procedural requirements, which is all this
Court may assess. The objects of the sections authorizing regulations are
ascertainable, and there is accordingly a basis for legal debate.

Disposition

[
200
]

The applicants submissions on the “rule of law” issue are rejected.
The province has broad powers of delegation, which have not been exceeded here,
