and the impugned provisions are not vague, as the objects are ascertainable,
providing the possibility of a legal debate.

Issue #6

Is Bill 160 unconstitutional in conferring
upon the Minister of Finance powers with respect to taxation, including the
power to determine the amount thereof free from legislative scrutiny, debate
and approval, without the submission of a
“
Money
Bill
”
, thus constituting
“
taxation without representation
”
,
contrary to sections 53 and 54 and the Preamble of the
Constitution Act,
1867
?

Position of the Applicants

[
201
]

The applicants contend that section 257.12(1)(
b
) of the
Education
Act
is unconstitutional in that it empowers the Minister of Finance to
determine and impose the amount of taxes without reference to the Legislature,
contrary to
ss. 53
and
54
of the
Constitution Act, 1867
.
The applicants
submit that the effect of
ss. 53
and
54
is to require that money bills be
submitted to the Legislature for approval, that any revenue raising measure is
a money bill, and consequently, it is constitutionally impermissible to allow
the Minister of Finance to set tax rates through regulation.

Position of the Respondents

[
202
]

The respondents submit that a clear statutory delegation of taxing
power is not precluded by the constitutional principle that taxation may be
imposed only by an Act of the Legislature or Parliament. They further submit
that the constitutional principle merely prohibits the imposition of a tax in
the complete absence of statutory support for the tax, and that where a statute
clearly authorizes a subordinate body to impose a tax by regulation, then the
constitutional principle requiring statutory support for a tax is satisfied.

Analysis

[
203
]

Insofar as this argument deals with the question of permissible
delegation, much of the relevant analysis has already been performed above,
under the rubric of issue #5. It is not my intention to repeat any of that
analysis here. The present issue does, however, raise a rather novel or at
least, unusual point; the application of
ss. 53
and
54
. It is the effect of
these sections which I intend to address here.

The challenged section, s. 257.12(1)(
b
)
states:

257.12(1) The minister of Finance may make
regulations,

…

(b
)

prescribing
the tax rates for school purposes for the purposes of section 257.7.

[
204
]

Section 257.7 directs various bodies, such as municipalities and
district school boards to levy and collect the rate as set out in regulations
under s. 257.12.

[
205
]

The challenge to this section is grounded in
ss. 53
and
54
of
the
Constitution Act, 1867
,
which hold:

53. Bills for appropriating any Part of the
Public Revenue, or for imposing any Tax or Impost, shall originate in the House
of Commons.

54. It shall not be lawful for the House of
Commons to adopt or pass any Vote, Resolution, Address, or Bill for the
Appropriation of any Part of the Public Revenue, or of any Tax or Impost, to
any Purpose that has not been first recommended to that House by Message of the
Governor General in the Session in which such Vote, Resolution, Address or Bill
is proposed.

[
206
]

Sections 53 and 54 are made applicable to the Provinces by virtue of

s. 90
of the
Constitution Act, 1867
.

Case Law

[
207
]

While the provisions of
ss. 53
and
54
are rarely litigated, they
have not entirely escaped the notice of jurists.
The Royal Commission
Inquiry into Civil Rights
(“McRuer Commission”) (Toronto: Queen’s Printer,
1968), among its many tasks, considered the question of delegated taxation. The
Commission observed on this issue, at Volume 1, 351:

The general rule is that the Legislature is
presumed not to confer power to impose taxes or other levies or charges on a
subordinate legislator, even by general language such as is contained in the
Emergency Measures Act. By the Bill of Rights of 1689 [
sic
]

it is
provided that no money may be levied to the use of the Crown without the
consent of Parliament. The Legislature is presumed not to intend to override
this statute by a later statute by the use of general words. The power to
impose levies or affect existing levies may be expressly conferred.

[
208
]

The McRuer Commission did not find an absolute rule that taxation
could not be delegated, although, at 353, its recommendation was for a
restrictive approach:

Where charges or levies are authorized, the
amount should be fixed in the statute. General provisions for exemptions or
relief by regulation are undesirable and permit arbitrary discrimination. Where
such provisions are unavoidable, any exemptions, or exceptions granted by way
of relief, should be reported specially to the Legislature, as reports are
required to be made to Parliament under the Financial Administration Act, where
they may be scrutinized by the members of the legislature.

[
209
]

The text of the
Bill of Rights, 1688
(U.K.), 1 Wm. & M. (2nd Sess.), c. 2,
states:

4. That levying Money for or to the use of
the Crown, by Pretence of Prerogative, without Grant of Parliament, for longer
Time, or in other Manner than the same is or shall be granted, is illegal.

[
210
]

The McRuer Commission referred to the idea of legislative authority
for taxation as a presumption, and although it was against delegation of
taxation powers, it did not dwell on the implications of ss. 53-54. Case law on
the subject of
ss. 53
-
54
is scant. What exists is
obiter,
as the
mandatory nature of
ss. 53
-
54
has never been directly raised as the main issue
of a case.

[
211
]

In
The King v. National Fish Co
.,
1931 CanLII 726 (CA EXC)
, [1931] Ex. C.R. 75, a
regulation which provided for a licence fee per pound of fish caught was
challenged as being a tax, and not within the power of the Governor in Council
to enact. Audette J. struck the regulations down on other grounds, but made the
following comments, at 80, 81, 83:

Before approaching the question of the
amplitude of the power conferred upon the Governor in Council under the above
mentioned Act, it is well to state that the Parliament of Canada has
undoubtedly full and plenary power to legislate both in respect of the
provisions contained in the Act and in the Regulations, even if in the result
the tax or fee imposed were excessive, prohibitive or discriminative.

…

However, it is quite otherwise in the case
of a delegated power.

Statutory regulations differ from Statutes
in that it may be open to the judiciary to question their validity, to examine
if they have complied with the condition precedent, and if they are reasonable.
The Regulation cannot of its own inherent power control or originate matters of
taxation. Such an extreme step would be contrary, to the whole scheme and
spirit of the B.N.A. Act.

…

The Governor in Council has no power… to impose
taxes unless under authority specifically delegated to it by Statute. The power
of taxation is exclusively in Parliament.

[
212
]

I would note that despite Audette J.’s comments, he appears to
countenance an explicit delegation of the taxation power.

[
213
]

In
Chemicals,
noted above under issue #5, the Supreme Court
approved an extremely broad power of delegation. Duff C.J.C. did, however,
express some reservations about delegating the taxing power, at 253-254:

It must not, however, be taken for granted
that every matter within the jurisdiction of the Parliament of Canada, even in
ordinary times, could be validly committed by Parliament to the Executive for
legislative action in the case of an emergency.

It is not necessary for the purpose of the
present Reference to consider whether it is within the power of Parliament,
even in an emergency, to give authority to the Governor‑General in
Council to exercise legislative powers in relation to such matters as, for
example,
those within the scope of ss. 53 and 54 of the British North
America Act.
It is in the highest degree unlikely that any such question
will ever arise touching such matters. But it ought to be observed that, apart
from the conditions expressed in the
War Measures Act,
the validity of
any order, or regulation, made under the authority of s.3, is affected by a
two-fold condition: that it could be enacted as a statute, by Parliament, in
execution of its emergency powers, or otherwise; and furthermore, that
Parliament is not precluded by the
British North America Act,
or by any
later lawful enactment concerning its legislative powers, from committing the
subject matter of it to the Executive Government for legislative action. The
application of this two-fold condition does not require consideration on this
Reference. [Emphasis added.]

[
214
]

Sections 53 and 54 also came in for passing comment in
Reference
re: Canada Assistance Plan (B.C.)
(1991),
1991 CanLII 74 (SCC)
, 83 D.L.R. (4th) 297 (S.C.C.). The
thrust of the case was the attempt to apply the doctrine of legitimate
expectations to block a reduction in federal-provincial transfers. But, at 320,
Sopinka J. noted:

The formulation and introduction of a bill
are part of the legislative process with which the courts will not meddle. So
too is the purely procedural requirement in
s. 54
of the
Constitution
Act, 1867
.
That is not to say that this requirement is unnecessary; it must
be complied with to create fiscal legislation. But it is not the place of the
courts to interpose further procedural requirements in the legislative process.

[
215
]

To summarize, there is very little case law considering the impact
of ss. 53 and
54
on the power to delegate. What comment there is appears to
range from at least requiring an explicit provision for delegation of a
taxation, or, more restrictively, suggests such delegation is not possible
within the scope of ss. 53 and 54.

Implicit Repeal

[
216
]

It has been suggested that ss. 53 and
54
are not entrenched
provisions of the Constitution, and are therefore open to repeal, by either
Parliament, as it affects the federal sphere, or a provincial legislature,
which has the power to amend its own constitution. Based on this lack of
entrenchment, it has been suggested further that any delegation of a taxation
power is an implicit repeal, or at least an override for the purpose of the
specific legislation, of ss. 53 and 54, and is therefore acceptable.

[
217
]

The argument regarding implicit repeal was considered in
Reference
re: Agricultural Products Marketing Act
(1978),
1978 CanLII 10 (SCC)
, 84 D.L.R. (3d) 257
(S.C.C.). Laskin C.J.C., writing a judgment concurred in by three other members
of the Court, refused to consider the application of ss. 53 and
54
, holding
that the matter under consideration was clearly a fee, not a tax.

[
218
]

It should be noted that while Laskin C.J.C. did not specifically
comment on ss. 53 and
54
, he did consider the
Chemicals
case,
specifically the matter of “delegation in depth” and stated at 278 “I would not
limit its rationale to emergency legislation”. Thus, any attempt to distinguish
the extensive rule making power provided for by the
War Measures Act
as
an emergency measure, and not applicable to the peace time context, is not
entirely satisfactory.

[
219
]

Leaving aside the question of distinguishing the
War Measures
cases,
the other judgment in
Re Agricultural Products Marketing Act,
rendered
by Pigeon J., and concurred in by four other members of the Court, suggests the
possibility of implicit repeal. At 322 he stated:

I agree with the Chief Justice that
adjustment levies, as well as levies for expenses are not taxes. Furthermore,
ss. 53 and 54 are not entrenched provisions of the Constitution, they are
clearly within those parts which the Parliament of Canada is empowered to amend
by s. 91(1). Absent a special requirement such as in s. 2 of the
Canadian
Bill of Rights,
nothing prevents Parliament from indirectly amending ss. 53
and 54 by providing for the levy and appropriation of taxes in such manner as
it sees

fit, by delegation or otherwise.

[
220
]

Thus, Pigeon J. did not find it necessary to suggest that an
explicit override or repeal of ss. 53 and 54 was necessary., it would be
sufficient for an amendment to arise by necessary implication of the delegation
of a taxing power. Justice Pigeon’s comments are clearly
obiter,
and, in
my view, inconsistent with Justice Sopinka’s
obiter
comments in
Reference
re Canada Assistance Plan

that compliance with ss. 53 and 54 was a
necessary procedural step.

[
221
]

The implicit repeal approach has, however, received
obiter
approval
in the Ontario Court of Appeal, in
Eurig Estate (Re)
(1997),
1997 CanLII 1080 (ON CA)
, 31 O.R.
(3d) 777 (CA.). In that case, the applicant was seeking to characterize as a
tax what it viewed as an extremely excessive probate fee. The characterization
of a tax was rejected, but Justice McKinlay commented at 797:

…the fees in question are not taxes. I
refer to the reasons of Chief Justice Laskin in
Reference Re Agricultural
Products Marketing Act (
Canada
),
1978 CanLII 10 (SCC)
, [1978] 2 S.C.R. 1198 at p. 1129,
84 D.L.R. (3d) 257, holding that levies which were ingredients of a marketing
scheme were not covered by ss. 53 and 54. If the levies were to be considered
as taxes within these provisions, the
dicta
of Pigeon J. at p. 1291
in the same case on behalf of five members of the court, shows that there was
no transgression of ss. 53 and 54 by the delegation in question in this case.

[
222
]

The concept of implicit repeal has not passed without comment.
Professor Peter Hogg, in
Constitutional Law of Canada
at 352, refers to
the comments in
Reference Re Agricultural Products Marketing Act:

This [Pigeon J.’s
dicta
] seems an
unsatisfactory holding. Surely, the fact that the provisions can be amended by
the federal Parliament should not justify their disregard (as opposed to
explicit amendment or repeal) by the Parliament. Another possible answer to the
argument that ss. 53 and 54 prohibit delegation is that ss. 53 and 54 are
merely directory provisions addressed to the “internal” procedures of the House
of Commons and (like other such procedures) are not enforceable by the courts.
This answer is more plausible, but the presence of ss. 53 and 54 in the
Constitution
Act, 1867

suggest that they enjoy a higher status than internal
parliamentary procedure.

[
223
]

Similarly, John Mark Keyes, in
Executive Legislation: Delegated
Law Making by the Executive Branch
(Toronto: Butterworths, 1992) notes at
44:

…the Supreme Court in
R. v. Mercure
[(1988),

1988 CanLII 107 (SCC)
, 48 D.L.R. (4th) 1 (S.C.C.)] rejected this approach [implicit repeal] to the
repeal of constitutional provisions governing the publication of statutes in Saskatchewan. It is also difficult to
reconcile indirect amendment with
Reference Re
Manitoba
Language Rights (No. 1)
where the court rejected the notion that constitutional requirements
can be treated as “directory” when they are phrased in “mandatory” language.
Indirect amendment would effectively make the money bill provisions directory,
if not deprive them of legal effect altogether.

A more satisfactory approach to money bill
requirements is to apply them only in relation to enabling provisions. As long
as enabling provisions receive the royal recommendation, or are initiated in
the lower house, the requirements are met. Although this differs from the
approach taken to language requirements, they warrant different treatment when
one bears in mind their different purposes.

[
224
]

As Keyes notes, the approach taken to indirect amendment in
R. v.
Mercure

(1988),
1988 CanLII 107 (SCC)
, 48 D.L.R. (4th) 1 (S.C.C.), is clearly at odds with Justice
Pigeon’s
obiter
suggestions. In
Mercure
,
which took place in Saskatchewan, the accused argued that he
was entitled to a trial and copies of the provincial legislation in French. At
the Supreme Court level, the case focused on the same question as the Manitoba
Language Reference, whether statutes should have been published in French, and
the effect thereof. Section 110 of the
North-West Territories Act,
R.S.C.
1886, c. 50, provided for publication in French. Under the
Saskatchewan Act,

S.C. 1905, c. 42, the
Northwest Territories Act
was continued in
force, where it was not inconsistent with the
Saskatchewan
Act.
As such, s. 110 was open to
repeal, but, the
Saskatchewan Act
was silent on this particular French
language entitlement. The argument was made that s. 110 was implicitly
repealed by later practice. This proposition was rejected by La Forest J., at
64:

A basic provision regarding the manner in
which a legislature must enact laws cannot be ignored. I cannot accept that
such a provision can be impliedly repealed by statutes enacted in a manner
contrary to its requirements, particularly one that is aimed at an
accommodation of an historically sensitive matter like the use of the English
and French languages in this country. Since the manner and form of enactment
(in English and French) was not entrenched, however, the provisions may be
modified or repealed, but such repeal or modification must be made in the
manner and form required by the law at the time of the amendment.

[
225
]

La Forest J. also generally rejected the idea of implicit repeal as
applied to legislation of a constitutional nature, at 56:

The courts, and particularly this court,
have expressed themselves in even stronger terms in the area of law giving
expression to human rights which it has treated as being of an almost
constitutional nature. Repeal of such laws requires “clear legislative
pronouncement”, to use McIntyre J.’s words in
Re Winnipeg School Division No
1 and Craton
(1985),
1985 CanLII 48 (SCC)
, 21 D.L.R. (4th) 1 at pp. 5-6…

[
226
]

Given the more recent Supreme Court jurisprudence, I find the
implicit repeal argument to be unworkable. It may be that
s. 257.12
(
b
)
is acceptable delegation. It may be that the province could validly decide to
repeal ss. 53 and 54, as applied to Ontario, at least for the purposes of the
Education Act.
However, if
the section cannot stand on its own terms, it is my opinion that the
application of an implicit repeal doctrine to uphold the section would be
unsupportable.

[
227
]

As noted, any reference to implicit repeal has been
obiter.
In
both
Reference Re Agricultural Products Marketing Boards,
and
Eurig
Estate (Re)
,
the courts concerned found the items in issue to be fees, not
taxes. Furthermore, the consideration of ss. 53 and 54 took up very little part
of the judgments in those cases. Also, there are
obiter
judgments going
in roughly the opposite direction. Sopinka J., in
Reference Re Canada
Assistance Plan
suggested that s. 54 was a necessary procedural step.
To be fair, this did not play much of a role in the case, as with
Eurig
and

Agricultural Products.
Still, the idea of a necessary procedural step
seems to be at odds with any implicit repeal of that step.

[
228
]

More significantly, both Audette J. in
National Fish Co
.
and
Duff C.J.C. in
Chemicals,
attached quite a degree of importance to the
constitutional nature of ss. 53 and 54. That constitutional nature, in the
opinion of those judges, precluded any casual or less than explicit delegation
of the taxation power, at the very least. Surely the same must be true of any
repeal of those provisions. I only rely on
National Fish Co
.
and
Chemicals

to demonstrate the importance of ss. 53 and 54. They do not, after all,
make any direct reference to the implicit repeal concept. But, the combination
of those cases, in concert with the
Mercure

approach to implicit repeal,
suggests that for any constitutional provision, the implicit repeal analysis is
inapplicable.

[
229
]

On this question of implicit repeal, I am in full agreement with Professor
Hogg. The presence of ss. 53 and 54 in a constitutional document must mean
something, even if they are not entrenched.

Application of ss. 53 and 54

[
230
]

Although I reject the concept of implicit repeal, it does not follow
from this rejection that
Bill 160
violates the requirements of ss. 53
and 54. Further consideration of the purpose and context of these
sections is necessary.

[
231
]

It is clear from the citation above that Keyes does not appear to
attach much significance to Parliamentary scrutiny of taxing provisions. He
suggests that as long as the enabling provision has undergone legislative
consideration, a vague delegation of taxation power is acceptable. In contrast,
recall that the McRuer Commission was against any such delegation, a position
supported by Rene Dussault and Louis Borgeat in
Administrative Law: A
Treatise,
2nd ed. (Toronto: Carswell, 1985). At 446, 447, vol. 1 they
comment:

It was precisely the danger of confusing
these two closely related legal notions [taxes and fees] that led members of
the Special Committee on Statutory Instruments to suggest that “there should be
no authority to impose by regulation anything in the nature of a tax (as
distinct from the fixing of the amount of a licensing fee or the like). Where
the power to charge fees fixed by regulation is conferred, the purpose for
which the fees

are to be charged should be clearly expressed.”

This principle, which has been applied here
only to the power of charging licence or permit fees, must a
fortiori
be
applied to cases in which Parliament has delegated the power to raise taxes to
the Administration. Indeed, it is essential for the Legislature to be very
vigilant in order to keep intact, and in the hands of Parliament, control over
a power which may so directly affect the property of citizens.

[
232
]

These are, of course, merely submissions as to what the authors
recommend should be a government’s approach to this issue. The submissions are
not binding, but they do suggest that at a theoretical level, it may be unwise
to dismiss ss. 53 and 54 as mere procedural steps. While these provisions
certainly do not prevent a government from bringing in taxation measures, they
do perhaps provide a higher form of scrutiny and public awareness than might be
the case in government through regulation.

[
233
]

Too much should not be made of the public scrutiny argument. After
all, we have an extensive system of government by delegation, on matters
perhaps as important as taxation measures. Of course, unlike most government by
delegation, avoidance of the delegation of taxing provisions has been situated
in a constitutional document. The existence of ss. 53 and 54 entitle the
argument against delegated taxation to more judicial respect than arguments
against the delegation of power generally. Again, though, given the historical
context, one has to be careful about how far one takes the
constitutionalization argument.

[
234
]

Sections 53 and 54 have, as their direct antecedent, the
Bill of
Rights
of 1688. These provisions were aimed at the restriction of state
power, not its facilitation. The growth of the administrative state is a
twentieth century phenomenon. Arguably, the wealth of detail necessary for the
functioning of a modern state was not under consideration when the
Constitution
Act, 1867

was framed. Without reverting to an “intent of the framers”
orthodoxy, the point simply is, that while ss. 53 and 54 are entitled to
respect for their presence in a constitutional document, it would be
overstating the case to suggest that they are at the very heart and soul of the
Canadian Constitution, and should be jealously guarded as such.

[
235
]

These arguments lead me to the conclusion that it is necessary to
acknowledge the existence of ss. 53 and 54, and that they have some impact and
effect, albeit limited. While heed should be paid to the existence of ss. 53
and 54, their nature and history suggest that their requirements are
sufficiently satisfied when the delegation of the taxing power, in a bill
approved by the legislature, is clear and explicit, as it is in the present
case. This conclusion is consistent with the case law on these sections,
discussed above.

[
236
]

Also, reinforcing this conclusion is the submission of the
respondents that if the legislature could not delegate the power to tax, then
municipalities and school boards could themselves have no power to tax, since
their powers in this regard have historically been delegated to them by the
legislature.

[
237
]

I am in agreement with this submission. No case law was tendered to
the Court suggesting that school boards and municipalities could not validly
exercise a taxing power. Moreover, a brief review of the law of municipalities
gives no indication that there is anything in the least bit questionable about
a municipality—a delegate—exercising a taxing power.

[
238
]

The fact that the power of municipalities to tax does not appear to
have been challenged may not, on its own, be determinative. It is, however,
worthy of some weight, given the extensive jurisprudence in regard to
municipalities. More importantly, it is consistent with the other case law
dealing with ss. 53 and 54, which suggest clear and explicit delegation of the
taxing power is sufficient to satisfy those sections.

Disposition

[
239
]

The submission of the applicants that
Bill 160
constitutes a
contravention of
ss. 53
and
54
of the
Constitution Act, 1867

is
rejected. To satisfy the requirements of ss. 53 and 54 the delegation of the
taxing power must be express. Such is the case here, and consequently, the
applicants must fail on this ground.

Conclusion

[
240
]

The two applications considered involve several thousand pages of
evidence and authorities. The many issues are complex. The Court has been aided
considerably by the very comprehensive written and oral submissions made by all
counsel. The cooperation of all counsel in narrowing the issues and organizing
the evidence and arguments, coupled with their very able and thorough
presentations, was much appreciated and is acknowledged as very helpful.

[
241
]

For the reasons given, it is declared that
Bill 160
is
unconstitutional insofar as it removes or affects the right or privilege to tax
from the Roman Catholic Community with respect to their denominational schools,
as a violation of the
s. 93(1)
,
Constitution Act, 1867

guarantee.
It is declared that the
Education Act,
R.S.O. 1990, c. E. 2, as amended by
the
Education Quality Improvement Act, 1997,
S.O. 1997, c. 31, is of no
force and effect insofar as it relates to or affects the separate school system
in respect of the right or privilege to tax with respect to denominational
schools that is guaranteed by s. 93(1) of the
Constitution Act, 1867.

[
242
]

I may be spoken to further as to the implementation of this judgment
and as to the matter of costs, if necessary.

Applications granted.
